items.excerpt: New Jersey’s multifaceted world of underground music features a healthy amount of experimental jazz, mutating into various new and unique directions. items.body: New Jersey’s multifaceted world of underground music features a healthy amount of experimental jazz, mutating into various new and unique directions. In the same land that spawned Wayne Shorter, Sarah Vaughan and the famed Van Gelder studios, there seems to be an endless amount of artists pushing the boundaries on the genre today, from the hallucinatory prog-funk fusion of New Brunswick’s Guesstimate and Asbury Park’s We Used to Cut the Grass, to the improvisatory adventurousness of Paterson’s Thieves in Paris. Yet one name that always seems to appear while discussing the current state of Jersey jazz, and that is Mike Noordzy. From projects like El Noordzo, Mothguts and the Mike Noordzy Quintet, the Middlesex County-dwelling multi-instrumentalist never ceases to wow and amaze with his genre-defying sounds and unorthodox approaches. One of my favorite of his many albums was the shadowy avant-jazz soundscape that is Shark Funeral Songbook, released under his Noordzo moniker back in 2017. Nearly ten years later, he’s released a follow up, Shark Funeral Songbook Vol. 2, and it defied the odds and outshines the original. The album squirms and throbs with murky life, as it swings from percussion and string-based tracks that echo the works of Moondog, to surreal noir drifts and cataclysmic jazz-metal sludge and beyond. The album is a deep and varied collage of all kinds of styles and flavors, often blending and clashing together within a single track. The end result may offer hints of the likes of Tom Waits, Peter Brötzmann and, in the case of the harder tracks, Noordzy’s own Mothguts project, yet there is really no other album quite like this one. Between the collision of disparate genres, greasy textures, gritty atmospherics and unhinged rhythms all bleeding together within a very musique concrète-styled mix, this is a truly one-of-a-kind musical experience. The more you listen to this spooky record, the more you get pulled into its vastly immersive sonic world, and the more you feel like you’re getting a glimpse into the busy mind of a multifaceted artist who can channel their creativity into a thousand different directions at a moment’s notice. Boundless, unpredicatble and endlessly entertaining, Shark Funeral Songbook vol. 2 is a must have for fans of Sonny Sharrock, Colin Stetson and Moor Mother. Click here to get your copy today for Bandcamp Friday! -KH
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是新泽西多乐器演奏家迈克·努尔兹的续作，延续了前作《Shark Funeral Songbook》的暗色美学。整张作品呈现出极为驳杂的拼贴结构：在同一首曲目中，弦乐与打击乐的对话可能突然被无调性的噪音洪流切断；Moondog式的街头节奏与Peter Brötzmann般的自由即兴彼此交缠；爵士与金属的边界被反复跨越，声响在浓稠的质感与尖锐的嘶鸣之间持续切换。评论特别提到其混音手法带有具体音乐（musique concrète）的痕迹，不同质地、节奏和音色层叠渗透，形成一个沉浸感极强的暗黑声场。专辑从Tom Waits式的黑色叙事漂移到Sonny Sharrock式的猛烈爆发，每一曲都试图开拓新的方向，而非依赖既有类型框架。

items.body: Review by Cicero 3.14 — Among the recent live albums I've had the chance to review, some were accompanied by choreographedperformances that are hard to appreciate when you only have the audio. Yet, combining dance withprog for a unique evening seems to be a growing trend. This was the case for the wonderful livealbum by Ana�d, as well as Le Orme's *La Gondola*. So, where does this live album by Runaway Totem?aband with such a unique approach?fit in?Founded by Roberto Gottardi in 1988, RT has 14 albums to its name, including two live releases. Thisis the third?a double album. Initially classified as Zeuhl, RT was already transcending the genrewhen I saw them in 2015. At the time, the vocalist was Raffaello Regoli (frontman of Cormorano, whomI reviewed recently), and I was somewhat disappointed when I met the band the day after the concertand they asked for my opinion. In fact, I believe that having multiple creative forces involvedrequires a catalyst that is difficult to achieve. Roberto is now solely at the helm; this albumoffers greater coherence in showcasing the project's ambitions, and Andromaca?an experimentalItalian duo featuring Antonella Suella (vocals) and Stefano Bertoli (keyboards, programming,Ableton)?proves to be an excellent partner here. CD1 is titled *Searching for a New Dimension*; inhis brief stage introduction, Roberto mentions Krautrock, and that is indeed where one should lookfor points of reference. Electronic and psychedelic sounds, infused with Indian percussion andfeaturing distinct, unexpected nods?such as Pink Floyd's "On the Run" or Tangerine Dream's"Stratosfear"?blend naturally into this continuous 45-minute sequence. The final section, with itsguttural incantations, brings this first journey to a powerful and deeply soulful close. CD2, *Onthe Edge of Space and Time*, offers a series of tracks interspersed with Roberto's spokenintroductions; it includes "Heliocentric Energy," an enlightening vocal-versus-synth duel?a far cryfrom the Page/Plant dynamic! I'll wrap up there, as "enlightening" is exactly how I felt afterlistening to this album. Two hours spent in another world...Originaly published in french on Prog censor's FB pages

Andromaca 这张双碟现场专辑将Zeuhl框架下的实验精神与Krautrock电子迷幻脉络衔接。第一碟《Searching for a New Dimension》以连续四十五分钟不间断的形态铺陈，合成器质感与印度打击乐层次递进，Pink Floyd式音效碎片与Tangerine Dream式冷峻合成线条自然嵌入。第二碟《On the Edge of Space and Time》以分轨结构穿插主创人的现场口述，人声与键盘编程形成对峙式对话。客席实验双人组Andromaca的加入为乐队原本的强力风格注入电子编程与声音设计维度，Roberto全权主导后作品内在一致性显著提升。两小时的聆听体验聚焦于现场即兴与电子程序控制的交汇，是一张跨越多领域触觉的现场记录。

items.body: Mara gets to Germany and does well. She earns, she buys herself a BMW, and what she boasts about is the legroom: now she can spread her legs as far as she likes. Then the car dies on the Autobahn outside Munich. The crisis has eaten her savings, the job has gone and the visa with it, and she is sat in a car she can’t afford to move. “Mara” is the first single from Gastarbeiter, the third album by GORDAN, out on Glitterbeat on 20 November. Singer Svetlana Spajić found the whole story in two lines. A bećarac, ten syllables to a line, the rhyming couplets people trade at weddings and drinking sessions in the Posavina, the farming country along the river Sava in northern Bosnia, one singer calling and another answering back, usually to make a joke or land an insult. Hers was about a woman stuck on the Autobahn in a new car with no money, sending home for someone to come and get her. Spajić wrote the rest. She keeps that couplet running through the whole lyric. Each verse says its line, then says it again with the words swapped round, Mara sliding from the end of the line into the middle. It’s a story being retold, and it gets worse every time. Halfway through, the verb shifts under the repetition and Mara stops whining that she’s been robbed and starts screaming it. By the last verse she’s home in Bosnia with none of the Deutschmarks left, back to the convertible mark, the currency Bosnia brought in after the war and fixed to the German one at one to one. Mara is a gastarbeiter, a guest worker, and there’s a whole tradition of songs about people like her. West Germany coined the word in the 1960s, after Yugoslavia broke with the rest of the socialist bloc and signed a deal to send its workers north, and it stuck in the Balkans as something said behind a man’s back. Those workers sang about missing home, about the shift, about families split by a border and parents left in the village, and that’s the body of song Gastarbeiter takes its name from. On the album sleeve is Gvozden Leaves for Temporary Residence, Mića Popović‘s painting of an ordinary Yugoslav man. Temporary residence was the state’s phrase for going to work in Germany, and Popović, a dissident, put it in the title to mock it. Gordan came together in Berlin during lockdown. Svetlana Spajić brought thirty years of going out to villages across Serbia, Bosnia and Dalmatia, learning the songs from the singers who still hold them, one place at a time, because the next valley sings the same song differently. That work has taken her into projects with Marina Abramović, Robert Wilson and Antony and the Johnsons. Austrian drummer Andi Stecher and German bassist Guido Möbius come out of noise and minimalism instead, and they also work together as GAMS. The three of them made Down in the Meadow for Morphine Records in 2021 and a self-titled album for Glitterbeat in 2024. Listen to “Mara” HERE and pre-order Gastarbeiter THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Gordan – Mara appeared first on Rhythm Passport.
items._genre: world music / experimental / folk fusion / Balkan traditional
items._cn_summary: Gordan的专辑《Gastarbeiter》围绕波斯尼亚传统的bećarac民歌形式展开，歌手Svetlana Spajić从塞尔维亚、波黑及达尔马提亚的村庄中搜集整理这些十音节对句民歌，并将之置于柏林实验乐手Andi Stecher的鼓与Guido Möbius的贝斯之下。主打单曲《Mara》讲述一位波斯尼亚客籍工在德国经济危机中失去一切的循环叙事，每一次重复中动词悄然位移，从抱怨变为嘶吼。专辑封面采用Mića Popović的画作《Gvozden Leaves for Temporary Residence》，延续了南斯拉夫离散工人音乐传统的脉络。乐队融合了田野录音式的民间采集、噪音与极简主义的器乐基底，以及深厚的文化历史叙事，构成一次跨越巴尔干传统与欧洲实验音乐的场景交汇。

items.body: Neram Pularumbol (“As The Dawn Breaks”) finds Sunken Cages pulling the rhythmic traditions of South India into an electronic vocabulary of bass, drones, and fractured club music. The album opens in celebratory, ebullient mode with “Kerala”, before “Elephant Dance” raises the tempo and “Idakka” takes a more synthetic path, processing patterns from the traditional hourglass-shaped Kerala drum. Breath soon becomes almost as important as rhythm. On “Darantee”, featuring Kuza, vocal exhalations and percussion give the music a physicality that draws on the agricultural and folk roots of South India. The connection with Kerala runs throughout the record, particularly through the collective force of its percussion traditions. “Drum and Flowers” imagines Chenda drums within a celebratory night dance, their increasingly animated rhythms rubbing against darker industrial sounds. “Athiraavile” — Malayalam for “early in the morning” or “at the break of dawn” — shifts the scene towards daybreak, combining an unprocessed Chenda melam pattern with heavy electronic beats and Rani Jambak’s incantatory voice. Throughout, traditional instruments remain clearly audible even as their rhythmic properties are stretched, fragmented and repositioned. The second half effectively takes that process apart again through a substantial series of remixes. “Drum and Flowers” alone appears in three new iterations: Weldroid, Lila Tirando a Violeta and El Kontessa pull its rhythmic framework in sharply different directions, at points veering towards acid, jungle and deconstructed club music. The source material consequently keeps changing hands and contexts, with each version exposing possibilities latent in the original. For all its electronic density, Neram Pularumbol eventually circles back towards the physical act of playing. “Kerala (Moki McFly Remix)” brings proceedings to an apt conclusion, returning percussion to a more tactile foreground and introducing distinctly jazzy, free-form leanings. The album begins and ends with “Kerala”, but the intervening transformations ensure that the return doesn’t feel quite like arriving at the same place. photo by Mike Vanemon To find out more about the production process for the album, we got in touch directly with Ravish Momin (aka Sunken Cages). The liner notes to Neram Pularumbol use resynthesis not simply as an electronic process but as a metaphor for taking culture apart into its constituent elements and putting it together differently, in opposition to the idea of tradition as something “frozen, solidified and sanctified”. That does seem particularly audible on Neram Pularumbol, where South Indian instruments and rhythmic languages are present but rarely allowed to function as straightforward markers of heritage. What exactly are you trying to preserve when you dismantle and reconstruct a tradition in this way, and at what point does transformation become more important than recognisability? Does this also connect with what you have described elsewhere as “resynthesizing the traditional” and decolonising conventional ideas of so-called global music? Thanks for this great question! The best analogy to start with is to think of making a photocopy of a photocopy. Even 8-10 generations of copies later, they do not resemble the original, get distorted and warped, and perhaps even a new narrative emerges. This process itself is of deep interest to me and what I’m hoping to preserve. When I think of a rhythm I’ve learned in the past, it’s more about how I’m recalling it in the moment, with all the unconscious inspirations and changes that get added over time- to be left with a transformation that’s an impression, an organic reimagining- similar to what happens to our own memories over time. Furthermore, I’m taking these ‘resynthesized patterns’ and placing them in a new framework of synths, drones, and other electronic elements that I’ve absorbed, to create a new global-music that simply doesn’t rely on invoking the past. I need to be careful to add that all this does not mean a blatant disrespect of the culture and tradition, but to be left with recognizable elements-like the sounds and basic structure of a pattern- in an arrangement that may be unfamiliar. That’s where the decolonizing takes shape. Music is predicated on a dynamic process of growth and evolution, yet too often non-western artists are expected to be performative of their culture, and their use of contemporary technologies or drawing inspirations from western genres is considered disingenuous. Gatekeeping and branding from western ethnomusicologists and curators has a long problematic history, but I’ll leave that discussion for another time Neram Pularumbol is particularly rooted in the musical traditions of Kerala, from the title itself to “Idakka”, named after the hourglass-shaped drum associated with Kerala’s temple music. Yet you don’t present these traditions ethnographically or attempt to reproduce them faithfully: their rhythmic and timbral characteristics are broken apart and absorbed into electronics, bass and club structures. Which particular Kerala musical traditions, instruments or rhythmic practices fed into this album, and what is your own relationship to them? Are there elements that you consciously wanted to retain in recognisable form, and others that you felt could only remain alive by being transformed? Hopefully my previous response lends some insight to this question as well. To elaborate, I’ve always found group drumming to be powerful, an action of resistance and solidarity as well as of spiritual significance. Particularly, I was mesmerized by music performances known as Chenda melam in which hundreds of artists sync and perform together during temple festivals in Kerala. The drums native to Kerala, like the Chenda, Idakka and Elathalam, also have markedly different timbres/sonorities from the North-Indian drums such as Tabla and Dhol to which one may be accustomed to hearing. While I’m originally from South India (Hyderabad) myself, I currently split my time between Brooklyn and Philadelphia. I did not grow up in Kerala, India, but I wanted to think about what a meaningful recreation of those rituals into my own worldview, that was culturally respectful as well, would represent. For example, On “Drum and Flowers,” I created a narrative with shifting tempos where the Chenda drum is used in a celebratory night dance, after the workers have come home. A multitude of drums lead the celebrations, shedding industrial grime for synchronized movements that quicken, a shared bodily memory of ancestral resistance and resilience. The song is punctuated with industrial textures and dark synth stabs that represent the rigor of factory-work. “Idakka,” the track to which you’d alluded earlier, runs the Idakka drum patterns through various delays and echo filters to create this cavernous rhythmic feel where machine-like sounds are also ever-present. Here the traditional elements are drastically transformed and chopped up, signifying a not-too-distant future where machines threaten to take over humanity. On “Athiraavile,” which features the Indonesian producer/vocalist Rani Jambak, I actually used a clean / unprocessed Chenda melam pattern on top of heavy electronic beats. Here, Rani lends a shaman-like call to prayer- not belonging to any specific religious denomination- where people gather to play drums at dawn. The second half of the album effectively allows other artists to take your rhythmic material apart again. “Drum and Flowers” is especially revealing because Weldroid, Lila Tirando a Violeta and El Kontessa pull the same source towards very different rhythmic and electronic environments, while Masma Dream World and Moki McFly produce two strikingly different versions of “Kerala” and Kush Arora makes “Idakka” considerably harsher and more propulsive. You have said that these collaborators were chosen partly through relationships you have built with artists around the world who approach tradition as something mutable rather than fixed. When you heard the finished remixes, did any of them reveal something in your own compositions that you hadn’t realised was there? And does handing the music over to artists from such different cultural and musical contexts become another stage of the album’s idea of resynthesis? The remixes were as much a part of the album as the tracks. And a resounding yes to your observation of having these remixes represent a further reshaping of the source-material, as multiple layers of resynthesis now exist Each artist brought their respective cultural background, musical aesthetic and production style to the table. Back during the pandemic lockdown in 2020, I’d actively sought out remote collaborations with artists in different corners of the globe. I do want to emphasize that it was also important for me to support women artists, do my part to highlight them in a male-dominated electronic music scene. Over the years, I’ve maintained my goal of building a musical community with diverse collaborators who all take musical risks and blend the traditional to the digital in their own practice. As an artist with a remix track-record of my own (Babani Sound System, Batida’s Ikoqwe, Depeche Mode, dragonchild and Thollem), I’ve spent a lot of time listening to a given track to quickly hone in on elements that resonated with my aesthetic- whether it was a vocal phrase, a melody or a rhythmic motif. The objective was to take apart the original track and re-stitch it back together highlighting that chosen element, in ways that wouldn’t be predictable. El Kontessa added a doumbek pattern to the underlying rhythm and made it feel like it was always there, as if South Indian and Egyptian musicians jammed all the time. Masma Dream World took the drone elements of “Kerala” which I’d intentionally layered heavily, to create a very cinematic track with a stripped down minimal beat. Weldroid’s acid synths and bit-crushed elements gave the track a dance music of the future energy. Lila Tirando a Violeta removed my rhythmic elements entirely and energized the track with a Jungle vibe. Moki Mc Fly seemed to instinctively grasp my AACM past- which was grounded in their ancient to the future motto- and brought an acoustic Free-Jazz tribute to the Art Ensemble of Chicago to his remix. Neram Pularumbol means “As The Dawn Breaks”, while the name Sunken Cages itself has a much darker environmental origin: you have described the “sunken cage” as an image of something once held captive becoming submerged by rising waters, reflecting your background in environmental engineering and longstanding concern with climate change. Yet this record often feels less apocalyptic than that image suggests: despite the drones, industrial textures and moments of considerable darkness, there is movement, colour and a sense of emergence. What does “dawn” mean within this record? Is it intended as a counterweight to the darker implications of Sunken Cages, or do you see destruction, transformation and renewal as parts of the same process? For the past few years, I’ve been thinking a lot about the duality of the nature of water, as a source of survival and also as one of destruction. While there is a sense of hopelessness that comes from realizing that some of the impacts of climate-change are irreversible, there is also hope in focussing on environmentally sustainable practices. Rather than thinking of dawn as a counterweight to the bleakness of the overarching climate narrative, I wanted to leave its symbolism ambiguous. In other words, we can meet the dawn feeling powerless or prepare to transform our future for preservation. On a broader level, the choice still doesn’t seem to have been made. As far as the tracks go, I play with the tension between the forces of darkness and rejuvenation- with the industrial sounds/textures on the verge of overpowering the ancient rhythms and chants, which signify our humanity, and certainly different tracks allude to different outcomes of that struggle. PS. Since this interview took place, Momin has released Morning Birds and Distant Drums, a new album with Haitian “soundchemist” Val Jeanty as Turning Jewels Into Water. Taking the AACM credo “Ancient to the Future” as a guiding principle, the record brings their Indian and Haitian lineages into a kinetic dialogue with improvisation and contemporary electronics. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: Sunken Cages的《Neram Pularumbol》将南印度的传统节奏体系——包括Chenda鼓、Idakka鼓及民间声乐——置入电子音乐语境中进行解构与重塑。专辑以'Kerala'开篇，营造庆典氛围，随后通过'Idakka'和'Darantee'等曲目展示合成器处理与呼吸声在节奏中的重要性。'Drum and Flowers'将传统鼓声与工业暗色声响并置，'Athiraavile'则结合未经处理的Chenda节奏型与沉重电子节拍。专辑后半部分是多位电子音乐人（Weldroid、Lila Tirando a Violeta、El Kontessa）对该作品的多次重混，触及acid、jungle与解构俱乐部音乐等多种风格。整体创作理念以'resynthesis'为隐喻，主张将文化拆解重组而非将其固化为博物馆式的传统符号，强调传统乐器在变形中仍保持可辨性。

items.body: Review by Logan — The ambient, coolly nostalgic opening sequence of Geogaddi indicates the record's direction. Adjusting to the full album required some acclimation after years of listening to Music Has the Right to Children, but many elements appealed to me right away. Taking some distance from the debut allowed this strange, isolated world to make sense."Music Is Math" and "1969" rely on steady, ticking beats reminiscent of the D�sseldorf electronic scene, but with an uneasy feeling underneath. Further into the tracklist, pieces like "The Beach at Redpoint", "Gyroscope", and "Alpha and Omega" shift toward a darker Krautrock friction. The record relies on hypnotic, repetitive loops rather than traditional musical showmanship, focusing on old-sounding, distorted analog textures.My first favourite was clearly Music Has the Right to Children, which I found immediately accessible, followed by The Campfire Headphase, though I still loved Geogaddi during that era. However, it was only after Inferno came out that I deeply loved the final three albums, and the early material became more distant to me. This record is more like a 4.5 for me, though it gets a rounded-down 4 for Prog Archives purposes. Geogaddi is a strong exercise in sound design, but it remains a step below those late-career masterpieces for me. Inferno, The Campfire Headphase, and Tomorrow's Harvest mean the most to me these days, but all of Boards of Canada's albums I consider to be masterpieces in their own ways.Key tracks for me: "The Beach at Redpoint" and "Music is Math".
items._cn_summary: Boards of Canada 的第二张专辑《Geogaddi》延续了首张作品的环境电子路线，但风格更为幽暗与实验化。专辑以冷调怀旧的开场铺陈氛围，节拍稳定的作品如《Music Is Math》和《1969》带有杜塞尔多夫电子场景的影响，底层潜伏不安的张力；后续曲目《The Beach at Redpoint》《Gyroscope》《Alpha and Omega》转向更暗沉的德国摇滚式摩擦感。整张专辑依赖催眠式循环和老式失真模拟质感，而非传统音乐技巧，强调声音设计本身。评论者认为该作需脱离首张作品的预期才能理解其疏离而奇异的世界观，虽属杰作但略逊于乐队后期的三部作品。

items.body: An ache moves forward He steps back I step forward It all turns black He steps forward I step back Some relationships develop their own terrible choreography: one person advances, the other retreats, and a moment of contact sends both back through the same steps. On Annihilate, underground post-industrial producer and vocalist Lana Del Rabies gives that exhausted dance a setting of metallic percussion, dissonant strings, and voices that seem to drift through the walls. The prospect of closeness carries a threat of disappearance, as though reaching for another person might cost you the outline of yourself. Released through her own Feral Crone Recordings, the single revisits the gothic industrial territory of her 2023 album STREGA BEATA. Among her most accessible recordings to date, Annihilate brings its melody into clearer view within a dense, unsettling arrangement, with echoes of mid-career Nine Inch Nails, early Chelsea Wolfe, Dead Can Dance, and Godflesh. Written and produced by Lana Del Rabies, the track features bass, guitar, and additional instrumentation from Zach Wise, formerly of experimental black metal band Hissing. Deeply reverberant string tones open the song, their discord setting the room askew before a soft metallic beat begins carrying it forward. Creaking noises punctuate the haze, while thudding distortion stays buried beneath the mix, suggesting a heartbeat accelerating at the approach of something unwelcome. Her singing is soft, breathy, and eerily close; farther away, wails stretch across the recording like cries attempting to reach the living. The whole thing suggests a deserted Victorian factory, its decaying rooms still occupied by machinery and something considerably harder to identify. That dusty, corroded atmosphere recalls the gothic industrial aesthetics of the 1990s, with every small sound acquiring an uncomfortable physical presence. The lyrics begin with images converging in reverse and a moment suspended in time. From there, the exchange becomes a sequence of opposing movements: his withdrawal prompts her advance, his approach sends her backward. “Push pull fade” reduces the relationship to its recurring mechanism. Hearing her name briefly promises recognition, but the next attempt at contact leaves her grasping in vain. By the time the title enters the refrain, desire reads as a force capable of wearing away the person who feels it. Directed and edited by Lana Del Rabies/Sam An, the video translates that instability into grainy woodland footage, overlapping figures, and close-ups that dissolve before they can offer much certainty. Pale dresses and fabric catch the light against dense foliage; raised arms, blurred faces, and bodies close to the ground recur through successive layers of exposure. Black-and-white images give way to smeared color, turning the setting into something resembling a damaged reel of folk horror. The footage was shot by Jane Slater, whose video credits include Dildox, Brood Faye, and Sacred Skin, and Vox Porter of Sleek Teeth. Watch the video for Annihilate below: Lana Del Rabies began with early experiments sampling female pop musicians into noise tracks, a practice reflected in the project’s name. An has since developed a body of work spanning industrial music, gothic electronics, and experimental heaviness, examining human brutality and the prospect of apocalypse. Her recordings have earned attention from The Quietus, Metal Hammer, and Anthony Fantano, while her live performances have taken her to festivals including Roadburn, Coldwaves, Sled Island, Prepare the Ground, Northwest Terror Fest, and Soulcrusher. She has toured with Author & Punisher, 3TEETH, Pharmakon, JPEGMAFIA, and John Wiese, and opened shows for artists including clipping., Midwife, HEALTH, and Bell Witch. In 2025, An founded the art-focused label Feral Crone Recordings and released Le Temps Viendra and Omnipotent Fuck. She is currently working on a studio record with former members of Hissing, due in 2027. Listen to Annihilate below and order the single here. Annihilate by Lana Del Rabies Lana Del Rabies joins gothic rock vocalist Echos for a West Coast tour this October. items._cn_summary: Lana Del Rabies 的单曲《Annihilate》以金属打击乐、不协和弦乐与仿佛穿墙而过的嗓音构建出一个濒临消失的亲密空间，延续了2023年专辑《STREGA BEATA》的哥特工业路线。歌曲描写一段关系中反复推拉的对位舞步：一方前进、另一方后退，每一次接近都伴随自我轮廓被磨损的恐惧。回响深远的弦乐在开篇铺陈出不稳定的室内感，低沉的失真脉冲隐于混音底层，暗示心跳的加速。制作上邀请前黑金属乐队 Hissing 的 Zach Wise 贡献贝斯与吉他，她本人担任词曲与制作。歌词将欲望简化为反复发作的机制，而同名 MV 由她和 Sam An 执导，以颗粒感强烈的林间影像、黑白与涂抹色彩的交替层叠，把这种心理失衡转化为民间恐怖式的视觉废墟。整体保留了九十年代哥特工业的腐蚀质感，同时在旋律呈现上更为清晰可辨。

items.body: Lift the veil, see what I’ve become An exoskeletal pantheon Born again from bone and breath To spread the living gospel of death On Tears for the Dying‘s blistering new gothic track Devour Me, Adria Stembridge drags the band back toward its earlier roots with a slower, heavier gait, then breaks that crawl apart with abrupt tempo changes that make the song feel unstable beneath your feet. Stembridge handles drum machine, guitar, bass, and vocals, building the track from dark guitar figures, blunt low-end pressure, and drums that move with the patience of something following you home. Her vocals hang above it all in a cold echo, less concerned with theatrical grandstanding than with letting the words rot in the air for a second before the next image lands. You can hear Bauhaus in the skeletal guitar work, Alien Sex Fiend in the queasy theatricality, and PiL and Fields of the Nephilim in the sense that somebody has wandered far enough from civilization to start inventing a religion. That religious impulse becomes central once the lyrics start opening the trapdoor. Stembridge draws from cosmic horror, but the terror here feels brutally physical. A solitary figure encounters an impossible swarm, loses control of the body piece by piece, and becomes host to something that treats flesh as raw material. Bones break. Insects burrow. The victim survives only in the technical sense, gradually becoming an alien deity whose transformation has erased whatever person existed before. The nastiest idea arrives afterward: worship. What begins as predation becomes conversion, and the ruined body becomes scripture. Consumption, reproduction, faith, and extermination collapse together until divinity itself starts looking like another parasitic infection. There is something wonderfully foul about that conception of godhood, especially coming from a band whose Southern gothic deathrock has long carried radical queer politics alongside its horror imagery. Authority here comes crawling out of meat. The slower passages give those images room to breathe before the faster sections shove everything toward panic. That contrast is crucial. Speed alone would turn the song into pursuit; the deliberate sections make you wait for whatever is chewing through the floorboards. By the final transformation, cosmic horror has lost every trace of abstraction. Infinity sprouts mandibles, theology breeds larvae, and salvation becomes a forced rebirth inside a body that has been converted into temple, nursery, and weapon. Listen to Devour Me below and order the single here. items._cn_summary: 这张单曲以哥特死亡摇滚为骨架，将宇宙恐怖意象注入南方哥特美学。主创Adria Stembridge一人操控鼓机、吉他、贝斯与唱机，编织出骨骼般的吉他线条与沉重低频，节奏如尾随猎物的耐性般爬行。歌曲通过突然的节奏断裂制造不稳定感，慢板段落给予恐怖意象呼吸空间，快段则推向恐慌。歌词将掠食转化为信仰，肉体沦为经文，神性被描绘为寄生感染，宇宙恐怖的抽象性被彻底肉身化。Bauhaus式骨架吉他与Alien Sex Fiend式的病态戏剧性在此交汇，酷儿政治潜台词贯穿于骇人画面之下，构成对权威与宗教的双重颠覆。

items.body: When John Coltrane died in 1967 the jazz world felt a startling void. With the release of Expression , Coltrane’s final studio album, it must have felt like a narrative had been cut short of its intended ending. After all, unless Trane had recorded material that had never been released, that was it: no more new music from John Coltrane. We know the story 100 years after Trane’s birth, however. And did he ever record material that had yet to be released! Alice Coltrane worked relentlessly to preserve John’s towering musical legacy, and we know from Andy Beta’s incisive book on her life that after a long day of raising four children on her own, she would put the kids to bed, sit in meditation, and practice the music that meant so much to her and her late husband. What she also did was listen to unreleased recordings by John and prepare them for release. Among the recordings made public in the immediate years following John’s passing were two absolutely stunning (I can’t emphasize this word enough– stunning! ) recordings by the famed Classic Quartet of Trane, McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison, and Elvin Jones: Transition in 1970 and Sun Ship in 1971. Transition McCoy Tyner related to writer David Wild that sometimes John would give them two notes, or maybe just a scale, as the basis of a composition before they recorded. The title track to the album Transition, recorded in the spring of 1965 , certainly could be such a piece. The work features a tightly focused quartet that absolutely opens up the gates and begins to tear down the fences. “Transition” is one the group’s wildest, most ferociously open pieces. It’s as though the catalytic power of Ascension or Om has been concentrated into a narrow and controlled conduit. Both the kinetic energy coursing through that conduit and the narrowness of the channel itself create the conditions for tension and combustion. The “Prayer and Meditation Suite,” on the other hand, is an absolute masterwork. I am of the persuasion that comparing works of Trane to other periods in his life can dangerously undervalue some of his accomplishments. Any suite, be it Meditations or “Prayer and Meditation” would beg comparison with A Love Supreme . Forget all that. “Prayer and Meditation” would stand as one the great works in the jazz canon if it were the only piece Coltrane and the Quartet created. Movement II: “Peace and After” is the sound of a quest for peace complete with all the pain inherent in that search. Movement IV: “Affirmation” picks up where “Transition” left off and rings with crisis, explosiveness, and spiritual urgency. Violence was always slinking nearby during Coltrane’s life, as it is for us today, and his music embraces this reality, but I would never describe his music as “violent.” Just note the third remaining song on Transition : “Dear Lord.” It is hard for me to imagine there ever existed a world without this vulnerable dedication to peace. Urgency and catharsis. Peace and vulnerability. The circumstances without and the transition within. Sun Ship In the nighttime hours of August 26, 1965, John Coltrane and his classic quartet walked into an East Manhattan studio. That year Martin Luther King and hundreds of peaceful protestors were arrested in Selma for wanting voter registration fairness. Malcolm X was shot to death. The first massive contingent of US ground troops landed in Vietnam, and the United States would slaughter tens of thousands of people before the year ended using machine guns and missiles fired from military jets. In Los Angeles, unemployment rates for black Americans grew to levels greater than during the Great Depression, housing discrimination was bolstered by law, and Watts exploded in rioting after a violent encounter between police and a black man. John Coltrane placed his mouth around his horn and blew. The sound that emerged, a passage of lyrical melody deeply tender and filled with solace, titled “Dearly Beloved,” lifted into the air. John embodied serenity and the path to it. People were dying and being denied their humanity by a power structure that required their destruction, and John never pretended this was not the case. The path to peace traveled through pain, not around it. People are dying right now as you read this, but life’s powerful play goes on, in all of its tragedy and real joy. Afterall, John’s baby boy Ravi had just been born, and John had assembled this collection of musicians to record at night because that day he was busy celebrating his first son, John Jr. 's, first birthday. Attaining does not come without suffering, but it also arrives with beauty. Attaining. Sun Ship. Ascent. Amen. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了约翰·科川在1965年至1966年间与经典四重奏录制的两张后期专辑《Transition》和《Sun Ship》，由遗孀爱丽丝·科川整理后于1970和1971年发行。评论聚焦于科川晚期作品中将《Ascension》式的密集能量收束于狭小通道的创作手法，标题曲《Transition》展现四重奏极度开放、撕破边界的即兴张力。《Prayer and Meditation Suite》被视为可与《A Love Supreme》比肩的杰作，第二乐章《Peace and After》在追寻宁静中承载痛苦，第四乐章《Affirmation》延续危机感与精神紧迫性。《Dear Lord》则以脆弱的祈愿呈现对和平的执着。整体体现了科川将精神性、暴力张力与平和渴望融为一体的晚期美学。

items.body: “We fear the abyss called death because of a lack of imagination. Give up your death! Other dimensions exist beyond this material world, and the people there are shining a light for us to follow” Around the time of Hallowe’en and Dia de los Muertos, the spirit world shuffles towards the living, and its inhabitants carry glowing lanterns to light the way. As afternoons succumb to longer nights, the decidedly chilly winds of November require thicker coats as they rattle the bones, and the frights of October fade away. Some spirits still linger; they make themselves known through Tape Loop Orchestra’s music, like the senile smell of a perfume from the 1940’s. Some of them take up residence inside The Invisibles, working their way into the very fabric of the music, but other phantoms share the space, too. They’re artificially created, spooling out of a recurring nightmare’s webbed strands and surreal scenarios. The notes are fragile and transparent, and an almost ethereal atmosphere blows over the music like a cloud of cigarette smoke. Right from the off, the vocals of Beth Roberts haunt The Invisibles, settling down in a cool space, as if seated on the periphery of a dead nightclub. Shrouded in fog, the stalker that we call death suspends itself over the music, circling its next, clueless victim like a grotesque disco ball. Her striking lyricism soon loops and decays, and like a disintegrating memory her sturdy and strong voice begins to lose its once-reliable, storm-proof sound. It slowly shrinks and wastes away, like an underused muscle, losing its physicality, becoming spirit. Her held notes are like long strands of ectoplasm that so famously spluttered out of the mouth during private séances in the Victorian era. And the music is covered in a swollen layer of century-old dust, its skin permanently mummified. The processed strings try to emit their own kind of weak radiance – they’re used to shining brightly – but even these have grown pale. Something intangible rubs against the music, making The Invisibles less of a faked episode of Most Haunted and more of an authentic paranormal investigation. Her voice chants its hymn, spreading as if from a localized infection. When the vocals fade away, they drift into the unknown and their absence creates a presence. The strings slowly swell, swirling and roiling in the murky tempest that engulfs life and death. The notes waver, staggering through the ambient-lit fog, zombie-like. They wear a cloak, and they drape themselves over the fog. On Side Two, the notes are even thinner. The ice is crackling in the background, and the tones are close to disintegrating. An angelic chorus appears, trying to lift the music up and embalming it with its layers of vocal honey. Over the years, so many people have claimed to have seen a tunnel of white light as their own near-death experiences were recounted, and now this light hovers over the music. The disembodied spirit looks down on a temporary vessel it used to call home. All the saints are here, and it doesn’t matter if they’re the illusions of a misfiring brain. They’re with you, and that’s what matters. Death stalks the music as the misty-grey tones sit underneath the vocals, acting like lamp posts that illuminate inner circles of safe light to counteract a world perpetually suffocated by darkness and cruelty. The music isn’t here to hurt. It’s like a lantern, lighting the way for a smooth, liquid returning. Available through Boomkat on 11.11.16 www.oursmallideas.tumblr.com
items._cn_summary: Tape Loop Orchestra 的《The Invisibles》是一张围绕万圣节与亡灵节氛围展开的氛围/磁带音乐专辑，乐评以丰富意象描绘其声音特质：Beth Roberts 的人声如幽魂般盘旋，循环并逐渐衰减，仿佛维多利亚时代降灵会中喷涌的灵质；经过处理后的弦乐试图发出微弱光芒，却苍白失色，笼罩在百年灰尘之下。整张专辑被笼罩在雾气、腐朽与超自然气息中，音乐质地脆弱透明，如香烟烟雾般飘渺。第二面音符更加稀薄，冰裂声在背景中作响，天使般的合唱试图将音乐托起，象征濒死体验中的白光。评论将专辑比作一场真实的超自然调查而非作秀节目，强调其声音中那种有形与无形交织的特质。专辑融合人声、弦乐、磁带循环与环境氛围，呈现出死亡、记忆与灵性之间的模糊地带。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items._cn_summary: 《Palagoma》是内罗毕新厂牌Cool Waters的首发作品，由德国出生、肯尼亚定居的打击乐手Sven Kacirek与Olith Ratengo组成的二人组Odd Okoddo，邀来83岁传统肯尼亚东部的dodo歌唱传承人Ogoya Nengo共同录制。Nengo的加入为作品注入了深厚的传统根基，其演唱承载着肯尼亚数十年乃至数百年的声乐遗产，与Ratengo之间形成了跨越代际的声线呼应。Kacirek以Buchla合成器、手打打击乐及零星的架子鼓构建声音基底，电子层次缓缓铺陈，在不喧宾夺主的前提下为传统人声提供推进力。以《Bara》为例，反复的打击短句起初与人声形成僵硬对照，但合成器多层次复节奏渐次叠加，使声音在不知不觉中融为一体。整张专辑体现了文化之间真诚的对话与碰撞——根源音乐走向前卫，前卫声响仿佛传承千年。

items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Dorothy Moskowitz与作曲家Paladino、诗人Ferrari合作的实验性作品，融合前卫、氛围与调式音乐元素。钢琴作为核心乐器贯穿全作，时而与弦乐、木管、合成器交织形成相位偏移的复杂织体，刻意打破西方听众对和声进行的固有认知。Melody不遵循传统调性逻辑，而是围绕每个歌词的语义展开，Moskowitz的声线承载着哲学化的歌词，既有对美国当下政治极化、法西斯主义抬头的直接控诉，也有对死亡与人类在宇宙中位置的冥想。音乐风格被比作Steve Reich与Philip Glass式的极简重复美学，歌词传统则延续1960年代抗议歌曲的血脉。整张专辑介于歌曲与反歌曲之间，呈现出一种古老而陌生的音乐叙事可能性。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items._cn_summary: Tako Toki 乐队的这张专辑延续了其首作的风格拼贴路线，最大特色在于乐器本身——所有演奏器材均由废弃杂物手工打造，他们称之为 tassofon、kitchenofon 等自造乐器。尽管材质简陋，这些自制乐器的音准却相当稳定，在高品质录音下呈现出丰富的声学质感。曲目跨越多种世界音乐风格：克莱兹默的欢笑单簧管与巴松管对话，昆比亚风格的西班牙合唱与拉丁打击乐层叠，非洲节拍中的木鱼与沙锤环绕马林巴琴旋律，桑巴与中东调式交替出现。即兴段落展现出扎实的演奏功底，旋律线常以爵士化的切分与节拍形成张力。专辑展现了跨文化音乐语汇的融合能力，同时也隐含着对乐器本质的反思：当音乐人面对千篇一律的成品乐器时，创作冲动依然能找到自己的表达路径。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家 Omar Sosa 的专辑《Sendas》在意大利 Fazioli 音乐厅完成两小时无脚本独奏即兴录音，后经后期制作叠加人声采样、打击乐、循环音效、田野录音与环境声响。专辑延续 Thelonious Monk 式的不重复理念，Sosa 自述刻意规避流派标签，试图将多元影响融为新的整体。制作过程中融入声带唱诵、低脉轮共振等元素，追求精神性与简约美学。文章引述大量艺术家自述，涵盖创作哲学与对音乐工业分类体系的反思，并以《Inside the Spirit》开场段落为例，描绘指尖拨弦、缓慢展开的声响空间与器乐共振质地。作为独立厂牌发行的独奏即兴作品，在实验爵士与世界音乐融合维度上具有清晰辨识度。

items.body: Is Woven Ground an EP with an accompanying film, or a film with an accompanying EP? We’ll leave it to the project’s viewers and listeners and to decide. Either way, Blair Coron‘s multi-media release is a treat for the eyes and ears, a celebration of Scottish forests, islands and glens, filled with lush instrumentation, poetry and harmony, coupled with sumptuous landscapes and insightful interviews. As Coron explains, “I could never say, ‘This song is the river’ or ‘these words are the forest’ … so I took my instruments and recording equipment and friends to the places I was writing about.” The landscapes are first seen from a moving car, then the disembarking, revealing the sounds of the village and the port. In the early minutes, Coron celebrates the gift of the Isle of Canna, a sacred trust and sanctuary. The cows seem as relaxed as the strings and historical piano, or the other way around. The views are bucolic, the pace of life unhurried, the area seemingly free from pollution, time in suspension. The natural soundscape is allowed to take center stage (more detectable in the film than the EP). In the first interview, one learns of apple trees fertilized by the bodies of seals. Farmland equipment lies abandoned; an ancient church stands witness. Local residents express pride in their location and history. Shoes off, windows open, Coron engages with the piano; “Isle of Canna, Midsummer, 5:54am, 2026” arrives a third of the way into the film, but is the EP’s opening piece, a love letter to the location. The next piece takes a little more work; a harmonium is not an easy instrument to move, especially across uneven terrain. The sprightly “Sgùrr A’ Mhaoraich” is performed by a babbling brook, with Charlie Stewart on the much more portable fiddle. The piece is an ode to the countryside and the flowing water, whose music never ends. As the camera zooms in to the reel-to-reel, the recording device begins to look like a stream. Coron sits outdoors at a table, reciting “Beneath Six Black Poplar Trees,” a poem that looks back to the dawn of creation, with creation itself the accompaniment. His voice is comforting, with gentle inflection that matches the spider webs undulating in the wind. The strings return, setting up the gorgeous closer, which includes Miwa Nagato-Apthorp and Zoe Bestel on layered vocals. “Hymn,” while not on the EP, is one of the highlights of the film (35:12-38:06, a music video on its own). An adjacent version was released on the Two Old Songs EP in April, the original on On the Nature of Things, but we like this choral version the best. For “Moon Lament,” the quartet sits in the woods, captivated and captivating, having become part of the visual and sonic scenery, melting into the forest like the voices of the water and the wind. This ebullient song is chased by warm laughter and the twittering of birds; the camera draws back, revealing canopies of green. Woven Ground the EP becomes a souvenir of Woven Ground the film. The images resurface when playing the music, stored in the memory as the seeds are stored in the earth. (Richard Allen)
items._genre: folk / ambient / field recording / modern composition
items._cn_summary: Blair Coron 的《Woven Ground》是一部多媒体作品，将EP与电影结合，以庆祝爱那岛的自然景观。音乐录制于实地，融合了钢琴、手风琴、小提琴等器乐与诗歌朗诵，强调自然声景的中心地位。专辑收录了现场录音与当地居民访谈，呈现出一种宁静而沉思的氛围，乐器与自然环境相互映衬。这种跨媒介的创作方式模糊了音乐与电影的界限，作品不仅是对苏格兰森林、岛屿的赞美，也是一次将声音与视觉深度融合的艺术实验。整体风格偏向氛围与田野录音，与现代古典和跨界融合相契合。

items.body: Review by alainPP — This EP marks a period of reflection following the departure of two band members, including Charlie. So, is it a transition or an evolution?"In a Fever Dream" is a gentle, melancholic acoustic track with whispered vocals, a fragile sound that develops into atmospheric djent metal with thunderous riffs and trip-hop influences. The lyrics explore a sense of disorientation?a sign of things to come? The contrast with the drum polyrhythms and savage growls, the restrained, solemn crescendo, and the surprising Ross, is striking. "Delirium" features a piercing, syncopated riff over an industrial beat and a Haken-esque chorus. The djent element returns on this tightly packed, flawless track, culminating in an explosive, exhilarating outro that launches into "Eclipsed by You," a slow-tempo track that veers between staccato metallic vocals, a deafening groove, and progressive keyboard electronics. The track is linear and highly professional, a testament to the innovative nature of this song, which balances unbridled gentleness with restrained violence."Bleeding Sky" boasts a subtle, syncopated groove and the ever-present vocals, a hallmark of this band. An ambient break reminds us that HAKEN has a distinctly modern prog-djent metal signature with its hypnotic crescendo. The crackling pads give way to cinematic, bucolic bird sounds. "Lotus," with its ethereal piano, offers a gentle opening; a captivating, hypnotic sound with an oppressive groove. The djent guitar enters over Ross's distant, trembling growl. The alternation between the break and the long, atmospheric drift sounds like a fresco faded by time, lacking in ferocity, and Ross's falsetto reinforces this ethereal, post-rock feel.HAKEN returns to visceral, more technical prog-metal. A deceptively complex album, far more intricate than it initially appears.
items._cn_summary: 这是HAKEN在两名成员（含Charlie）离队后推出的反思性EP。五首曲目在轻柔原声与重型djent金属之间反复切换，融入trip-hop节奏、工业节拍与氛围键盘，呈现清醒梦般的迷失感。首曲以低语人声开场，逐步发展为带咆哮的金属段落；第二首以切分吉他与爆炸性尾奏推动张力；后续曲目交替呈现渐进式键盘叙事、自然鸟鸣采样与后摇氛围铺垫，钢琴主题与失真人声并行。整体延续HAKEN标志性的现代prog-djent声响，但在旋律克制与暴力爆发之间寻求更精妙的平衡，结构表面流畅实则暗藏繁复层次。

items.body: Reflections on Stellar Regions (1967/1995) Around the end of the year 1995, a „new“ album of John Coltrane, posthumous of course, was announced to be released. Alice Coltrane(AC), generally referred to in the press as Coltrane‘s widow and archive keeper, had found a previously lost tape of a 1967 recording date (and given titles to the tracks), we learned. As a relative newbie to modern, avant-garde jazz, you would generally resort to sources like „Das Jazzbuch“ by acclaimed writer J.-E. Berendt from your local public library (in Lower Bavaria, in my case). As to Coltrane’s music, you would probably have already taken Soultrane and Blue Train as a starting point, passed by Giant Steps und initiated yourself into the Impulse-/classic quartet period with, for instance, Live at the Village Vanguard . You would have learned that A Love Supreme was the peak of his creative work and a great milestone of modern jazz in general. Going on further to Ascension , probably tempted by Mr Behrendt‘s description of it „as an orgasm lasting 40 minutes“, it was, however, not for me. It was simply too much for me to take at that time, especially the lack of any „song structure“, I did not find an orgasm, but a collective, cacophonic mess lasting 40 minutes, to be honest. With that background, learning that the announced release, titled Stellar Regions , was originally recorded in 1967, it caught my curiosity nonetheless. Not only was this my birth year, it would also be interesting to see: how had Coltrane developed from 1965 on? And, sadly, we could expect to listen to some of his last recorded music, just five months before his death, Some raw facts: All the music assembled on Stellar Regions was recorded in the Van Gelder Studio in one day’s work on 15 February 1967, and the released material comprises everything recorded in that session*, with his regular group members of that era: AC on piano, Jimmy Garrison (JG) on bass and Rashied Ali (RA) on drums. But at this date in the absence of saxophonist Pharoah Sanders(PS), thus reducing the late period quintet of Live at the Villard Vanguard Again! to a quartet. After this studio date, Coltrane would return there exactly one week later on 22 February for a duo recording with RA ( Interstellar Space ) and in March for three more tracks to be released in late September 1967 on Expression . All but one of the tracks on Stellar Regions were unreleased before (I knew none of it anyway), as #5 Offering had already been used to complete the Expression album. And by the way, the title track #3 (alternate take #9) was an early version of Venus from the duo session with RA one week later. What is going on here? Having my CD copy of Stellar Regions in hand, what did I get? As an obvious statement already from the back of the cover: Shortness. A return to a noticeable format and compositional structure. 11 tracks (including 3 alternate versions) with a maximum length of just under 9 minutes (#1 Seraphic Light ), well … that sounded fairly familiar to me, even compared to a Genesis or Dire Straits LP (which, in the meantime, had found a place a bit farther behind in the rack). On first listen: Conciseness. Cohesiveness. Control, even constraint. The contrast to Ascension and even more so (although unknown to me), the sprawling marathon improvisations of his live 1966 work (the non-stop concerts of the 1966 tour in Japan!), becomes evident from the start. These pieces are tighter and more concise, the emotional bursts more focused. Lyrical clarity. Spiritual atmosphere. Much to my surprise. While intense and free, these pieces are balanced with moments of meditative calm. I found lyrical beauty on #1 Seraphic Light , #5 Offering and #4 Iris - the latter being a gorgeous ballad, pleasant rediscovery on re-listening and easily the most traditionally and melodically accessible track on the album. Is it „free“ jazz“ actually? Is this free jazz, I wondered? While I have no doubt, that this is a true free jazz album and the right stuff for the readers and makers of the Free Jazz Blog , this album still sits quite on the border for me. Needless to say, by February 1967, Coltrane had abandoned traditional chord progressions and swing rhythms. Why it may justifiably be called free jazz: - The protagonist does of course not abandon the extended techniques he had developed over the years - overblowing, shrieking altissimo notes and multiphonics. - RA displays his non-metric drumming and plays multidirectional rhythms, creating a fluid, rolling wave of percussion rather than playing a traditional steady swing beat. - The musicians as a whole are not bound by traditional chord progressions. They play with harmonic openness, outside the conventional harmony. And what makes it distinct from other works of the period, so it may be not: - Unlike his live performances of this time, Stellar Regions has clear, distinct thematic melodies at the beginning and end of most tracks, providing structural anchors. - JG‘s bass playing also acts as a massive anchor. Because he uses repetitive and modal tools to anchor the root note, the musicians never fully detach from a tonal center. - AC‘s chord playing on piano provides a harp-like, meditative harmonic cushion. It is free-form, but it’s deeply melodic and highly tonal as well. Conclusion: Stellar Regions uses the vocabulary of free jazz (energy, microtonality, open rhythm, non-metrical drumming) but pours it into shorter, concise and deeply spiritual tone poems, finding a balance between freedom and structure. Instead of plainly breaking the rules or „tearing down walls“, it is all about using freedom to achieve an emotional and spiritual state. What stands out I like the more lyrical pieces on this album very much. They really define this album and give it a distinct place in Coltrane’s late period timeline. They a show us a side of Coltrane’s final months that makes already a shift to a more spiritual atmosphere. They touch my heart and make me wistfully curious if more of that kind would have come flowing out of that musician. Offering (# 5) is a majestic ballad, the emotional center of the session and arguably the most structurally complete composition on the album. The track opens with a beautiful, hymn-like melody, played on tenor with incredible tenderness, sounding like a religious lament. AC enters with resonant low-register block chords. Coltrane’s solo moves away from the melody into intense, microtonal and split-tones. However, because AC sustains chords instead of playing dissonant clusters, Coltrane’s own fiery playing never sounds angry or harsh, but soulful, like a spiritual cry. The track concludes with a return to the opening theme. By the time the melody returns, the storm has cleared, leaving a sense of exhausted peace. Seraphic Light (#1). If Offering is a grounded prayer, Seraphic Light, the album’s starter, is pure cosmic ascension. While it has a more active, rolling rhythm play from RA, it remains one of the most texturally dense tracks on the album. This track begins not with a saxophone melody but with a rumbling of drums and cymbals from RA. AC establishes a continuous tremolo on the piano, while JG plays an aggressive, bowing bass drone. RA provides a rapid, metrically free tapestry of cymbals and snaredrum hits throughout. When Coltrane enters on saxophone, he plays short, declarative motifs that rise upward in pitch, bypassing a traditional jazz melody entirely. On this track, AC abandons all traditional piano performance boundaries. She does not simply play chords to back up a soloist, but creates a massive swirl of sound. The track builds to a peak where Coltrane‘s solo moves into the stratosphere, played in the extreme altissimo register of his instrument. Yet even throughout this peak, JG‘s grounding bass and AC‘s rolling waves prevent the track from becoming exhausting. It remains radiant and luminous. Does this album show us a path to the (unrealized) future? Now, as this year marks the 100th anniversary of John Coltrane’s birth and these recordings are almost his last notes to be captured on tape, it is a compelling „what if“-question: Where would he likely have moved to from here? Does this February 1967 recording – especially its lyrical core (see above) - give us a blueprint of what would have come? That is open for debate. Coltrane, sadly, recorded this music just five months before his death. We will never definitely know for sure how his music would have evolved if he had lived on. In his Allmusic review (4 ½* by the way), Scott Yanow argues that Stellar Regions offers no real hints of a future path. However, it may as well be stated that these recordings „represent a suggestion of the evolution his music would have taken had his life not been cut so short“ (David S. Wild, author of the liner notes, June 1995). Stellar Regions implies that Coltrane was heading toward a "chamber free-jazz" where total freedom was guided by internal discipline and structured devotion. Also, Stellar Regions suggests that the 1970s version of John Coltrane would have been less aggressive and far more compositional, spiritual and influenced by eastern aesthetics. It would have been intriguing to see him join his wife Alice in making the shift to World and Spiritual Jazz. Coltrane was already moving toward the cross-cultural, transcendent, meditative music of the 1970s, as evidenced in Alice Coltrane‘s ( Journey in Satchidananda , 1971) and Pharoah Sanders‘ albums recorded after his death. This session from mid-February 1967 still proves that avant-garde music can be profoundly beautiful, universal and divine. *The liner notes from June 1995 by David S. Wild confirm that the track To Be , released on Expression , with Coltrane on flute and PS rejoining him on piccolo flute, was not actually recorded on that same date, although being credited to that date on its original release. Also note: a contemporary review in German by Konrad Heidkamp from 09.12.1995, DIE ZEIT 50/1995, is still available for registered readers of DIE ZEIT . --- Klaus Kitzinger, born in 1967 in Landshut, Lower Bavaria, Germany. Still lives and works there in his daytime job as a lawyer specializing in construction law. A faithful follower of FJB, he got his first hold of free jazz as a teenager in the early to mid 1980‘s, when one enthusiastic pub operator actually brought luminaries like Archie Shepp, Sam Rivers, Joseph Jarman, the Sun Ra Arkestra, Jimmy Lyons/Karen Borca and Andrew Cyrille (spelled „Grille“ in the local newspaper) to his provincial hometown. Besides free jazz, he has an interest in (nearly) everything related to Japanese culture, traditional and modern, thanks to being married to Yuka. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑记录了1967年Coltrane晚期的一次录音，在其逝世前五个月完成于Van Gelder Studio，仅一日录完所有曲目。与此前Ascension的密集噪音不同，这张作品呈现出明显的回归：短小精悍的结构，最长曲目不到9分钟，11首作品包含3个备选版本，重新找回可辨的曲式框架。乐队编制精简为四重奏——钢琴Alice Coltrane、贝斯Jimmy Garrison、鼓手Rashied Ali，缺少Pharoah Sanders。同周后的Interstellar Space二重奏及稍后Expression的三首录音共同构成Coltrane生命末期的最后录音档案。评论者以新听众视角出发，将此专辑视为探索Coltrane从1965年后音乐演变的入口，作品本身的克制与短小构成对前作极端自由爵士的反向修正，是理解其晚期美学转向的重要文本。

items._cn_summary: Anna Webber 的非编制乐团专辑以九重奏形式展开，融合了复杂的作曲技法与即兴元素。乐评指出作品在结构上具有学院派爵士的严谨性，复调段落层层交织，配器色彩罕见而丰富。乐曲虽以爵士为根基，却凭借充足的律动感与非常规和声走向，明显偏离传统爵士风格版图，进入更具实验性的领域。评论来自 Avant Music News 的月度回顾，对这张作品的作曲层次与音色探索给予了正面肯定，认为它在风格归属上具有很强的跨界模糊性，适合关注当代爵士与前卫音乐交汇的听众。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — As if setting out to provide a soundtrack for the atmosphere of their native Finland, with snowflakes falling and blanketing everything in White, Horte crafts a hypnotic soundscape using electronic elements and synthesizers. They create a downtempo vibe that occasionally flirts with Portishead-style trip-hop, yet later reveals a folk-hop intimacy reminiscent of The Beta Band.Vocalist Riikka Pekkala's voice seems to float, notably on the opening track, "Pelko Karistaa J'rjen," where echoes reverberate as "Ilman Nurkka" unfolds amidst samples and loops, sung in their native tongue. In an album defined by wintry textures and a palette of blues and whites, the track "Kilpemme" seems to mimic a thaw amidst guttural guitar sounds, evoking a sense of Nordic psychedelia. It is a landscape where we lose ourselves like early polar explorers illuminated by the aurora borealis; a rock sensibility permeates the electronic modernity of this unhurried atmosphere, frozen like a block of ice that preserves the life within, holding it in suspended animation, paradoxically enough."Valoa On Liikaa" seems to mark time like a clock; Riikka Pekkala's voice takes center stage, conveying a stark, pale quality that nonetheless carries an inherent strength. Repetition, acting much like a metronome, sets an unwavering rhythm for the vocal variations. It is at this point that the synthesizer evokes string sounds and an emotional peak occurs, as the opposing poles converge."The Earth Gives Silence to the Night" is a highly evocative title for the album; "Kun Joki Haihtuu" is a powerful track where the bass and drums kick in, as if they had been waiting for the moment to break the ice and shatter it into crystals. These are moods that music used to express differently, perhaps never before so raw and stripped-down, revealing nature itself at that precise instant when everything comes to a standstill."V'isty Tielt'" is the most rock-oriented track, yet it defies convention; it leans into a kind of Krautrock-style transgression where Riikka Pekkala's vocals, clean and pure, almost like a religious plea, contrast sharply with a gritty, powerful backing track that advances with a "scorched-earth" strategy, leaving nothing in its wake. As one of the album's most progressive tracks, everything here sounds analog; there even seems to be a Mellotron-style choir, despite no actual Mellotron being used, though the sound is certainly processed to evoke that effect. The highly groovy bassline plays a pivotal role, transforming the song into a prophetic experience."Konttaa, Ne Konttaa II" brings the album to a close with echoes and Riikka's voice promising an eternal return, the certainty that things remain in motion despite appearing motionless, like the trees and all the surrounding nature of which we, of course, are a part.
items._genre: post-rock / math rock / Nordic electronic / trip-hop / folk-hop
items._cn_summary: Horte 的这张专辑以芬兰冬日氛围为基调，用电子元素与合成器构建催眠式音景。Riikka Pekkala 的人声如漂浮于冰雪之上，以芬兰语演唱，散发出空灵质感。整体节奏偏慢速downtempo，偶尔流露Portishead式trip-hop的冷感与The Beta Band的民俗亲密感。吉他的粗粝音色暗示北欧迷幻色彩，Krautrock式的推进方式在部分曲目中制造强烈张力。贝斯线与鼓点打破静默时，如同冰层碎裂。模拟质感的合成器弦乐与类Mellotron合唱效果增添了古老仪式感。专辑将电子现代性与岩石乐感熔于一炉，在静止中暗含运动，在冰封中保存生命力，是一幅用声响绘制的极地声景图。

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Is CARDIACS a progressive rock band? The question, which may have sparked debate at one time, seems obsolete today. All we can say is that singer and guitarist Tim Smith?the band's longtime leader, its heart, mind, and soul, and now more than ever regarded as an exceptional English artist, more than five years after his passing?is a child of the vibrant prog universe that truly lives up to its name. He himself cited among his countless influences such legendary names as Genesis, Faust, Can, Gong, Zappa, and Gentle Giant?a fact confirmed by the album *A Little Man And A House And The Whole World Window*.From the very introduction of the excellent new version of the track "A Little Man and a House," it becomes clear that this album will be on an entirely different level than *Seaside*, their previous album released in 1983. The compositions date back to the previous three years, but the production is much richer than on *Seaside* and in no way tainted by the typical sound of the '80s. Musically, it's a true leap forward, with arrangements of unprecedented richness ("The Icing on the World"), sometimes bordering on unnecessary excess ("The Breakfast Line," saved by its impressive grand finale). The significant contribution of William D. Drake's keyboards (who joined the band in late 1983) is no small part of this, as the musician displays a boundless imagination that rivals Tim's. Drake also co-wrote two of the album's most progressive tracks: "I'm Eating in Bed," which appears as a bonus track?a surreal little nursery rhyme that could easily have fit on *Nursery Cryme* or *Foxtrot*; and "The Whole World Window," which closes the album in a rather unexpected way, bringing CARDIACS closer to King Crimson's *In The Court* with heavy use of mellotron, piano, and bombastic organ, thereby convincing us once and for all that this is one of the most important prog works of 1988.
items._cn_summary: 这是Cardiacs 1988年发行的专辑，相比前作在制作水准上实现显著跃升，编曲层次更为丰富丰满。评论指出乐队灵魂人物Tim Smith深受Genesis、Faust、Can、Gong、Zappa、Gentle Giant等多名前卫巨匠影响，新加入的键盘手William D. Drake以不逊于Tim的想象力拓展了音乐边界。专辑部分曲目的编配接近过度堆砌的边缘，但终曲The Whole World Window通过大量运用mellotron、钢琴与恢宏风琴，将卡迪克斯推向King Crimson《In The Court》的厚重质感，被视为该年度最重要的前卫摇滚作品之一。整体音乐框架仍扎根于前卫摇滚传统，但内部融合了实验摇滚的怪趣与Can一脉的krautrock律动，是一张在传统前卫疆域内大幅拓宽表达的专辑。

items.album: Wrocław 2026
items.excerpt: On 1 October 2026, Nachtmahr chose Poland to open the longest and largest tour in the project’s history: three consecutive club dates in Wrocław, Poznań and Warsaw, with Cygnosic and Bagger 258 joining the opening run before IMPERIVM continues further across Europe.
