items.body: On 1 October 2026, Nachtmahr chose Poland to open the longest and largest tour in the project’s history: three consecutive club dates in Wrocław, Poznań and Warsaw, with Cygnosic and Bagger 258 joining the opening run before IMPERIVM continues further across Europe. When Thomas Rainer and I spoke ahead of the tour, he admitted that beginning in Poland had originally been a logistical decision, but previous experience with Polish audiences made it an unexpectedly appropriate one. A new programme inevitably introduces a degree of uncertainty, and he expected the energy of the Polish crowd to remove it very quickly. Wrocław supplied a fairly emphatic confirmation. Three bands approached electronic physicality from markedly different directions, yet there was no weak transition between them. Bagger 258 worked through blunt rhythmic force, aggressive vocals and a very direct relationship with the dancefloor; Cygnosic loosened that geometry into something darker, broader and more fluid; Nachtmahr then inherited a room already fully activated and pushed it into a much less orderly state. The evening did not feel like a headliner plus obligatory support. Its construction mattered. And Wrocław really is being spoiled this autumn. The number of strong dark-electronic, industrial and gothic concerts passing through the city has reached the point where they are beginning to form a genuine season rather than a handful of unrelated bookings. This was another very persuasive addition. Bagger 258 Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil I should already have seen Bagger 258 at the NCN Warm-Up this year, but unfortunately missed them there, so Wrocław finally gave me the chance to catch up. It took very little time to understand what I had missed. The Augsburg duo, Nico von der Eisenmühle and Tim “Hacke” Schmelzer, released their debut album “Aufwärts gehts bergab” in February 2026. Its language places them firmly inside EBM: Arbeiterwut, Funktion, Kontrolle!, Werkshalle 4, “Körperkommando“, Schicht im Schacht. Machinery, work, discipline and repetitive physical action are everywhere in the imagery, while Nachtmahr themselves contributed a remix of “Werkshalle 4” to the record. Live, however, Bagger 258 were far more interesting than a catalogue of genre references might suggest. Their greatest strength was immediacy. The beats came down hard and square, the vocals had real abrasion to them, and yet the performance never became rigid. There was too much visible enjoyment onstage for that. The music was aggressive, but the aggression kept converting itself into movement. There is a considerable difference between performing the visual grammar of old-school EBM and actually making a room respond to it. Bagger 258 did the latter. The pulse was almost mechanically regular, but the communication around it was human, animated and frequently playful. They were not protecting a historical form. They were using it. For an opening band, they also did exactly what an opening band should do without ever seeming subordinate to what followed. The audience did not require a long negotiation before deciding whether it was ready to move. Bagger 258 established that physical vocabulary almost immediately, and by the end of the set the room had already shifted from people waiting for the main act into people actively participating in the evening. Rainer had told me before the tour that the right support band changes the condition in which a headliner encounters its audience. If someone else has already brought the room to a certain level, you do not have to begin from zero. Bagger 258 made the point rather convincingly. Absolute knockout. Cygnosic Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Cygnosic changed the type of pressure rather than reducing it. The Athens project of Georgios Psaroudakis has a long history within dark electro, with Psaroudakis writing, performing and producing the material himself. “Demystify”, released in 2023, was Cygnosic’s seventh full-length album, while 2025’s “Theorem” reconstructed existing Cygnosic pieces through metal arrangements and showed how naturally heavier structures can sit inside the project’s electronic identity. That breadth could be felt live. Compared with the harder edges of Bagger 258, Cygnosic sounded more fluid and spacious, but describing it simply as “gentler” would undersell what was happening. The force had merely changed direction. Instead of striking repeatedly at the centre, the arrangements seemed to spread across the room, gathering weight through layers, melody and continuity. There was more air inside the music and more room for individual elements to develop. The rhythms still carried the performance, but the relationship between rhythm and atmosphere was different. Movement became less regimented, more continuous. The set could be forceful without constantly attacking. That made Cygnosic particularly effective in the middle position. Bagger 258 had already established the body as the evening’s main point of communication; Cygnosic kept the body engaged while changing how it moved. The result was dynamic, dark and surprisingly graceful. It also prevented the three-band bill from becoming three variations on the same impact. By the time Cygnosic finished, the audience was still physically engaged but had travelled through a noticeably different emotional texture, leaving Nachtmahr with exactly the kind of room Thomas Rainer had spoken about before the tour: warmed up, responsive and ready to be pushed considerably further. Nachtmahr Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil When Thomas Rainer and I spoke for Side-Line in August, much of our conversation circled around a contradiction at the centre of Nachtmahr live. The project’s visual language is built from command, discipline, uniforms, hierarchy, severity and theatricalised authority. Producing that world requires enormous control: sound, lighting, costumes, movement, timing and musicianship all have to function together. Yet the result Nachtmahr seeks from the audience is almost the exact opposite. The crowd is invited to abandon restraint, surrender to rhythm and lose control inside something that has been very carefully controlled on its behalf. For Rainer, the construction starts with the songs themselves. As he told me then, “The setlist is the script for the movie we present every night on tour.” The first IMPERIVM show gave that sentence a much more concrete meaning. The album, released on 26 June 2026 through Trisol, develops methods Rainer had already begun testing on “Verboten!” rather than simply applying another layer of production to an established Nachtmahr template. In our interview, he described Verboten! not as the end point of an evolution but as the record that established the method for what followed. IMPERIVM takes that logic further while retaining the project’s unmistakable rhythmic and visual identity. Onstage, however, theory disappears very quickly behind physical action. Thomas Rainer commands a room in a way relatively few performers can. That is not simply another way of saying that he is charismatic. What impressed me was how actively he reads the response in front of him. A gesture produces a reaction; he catches that reaction and sends it back, larger. The next rhythmic hit strengthens it again. The relationship becomes circular rather than one-directional. In Wrocław, that feedback loop escalated with remarkable speed. The entire live formation is central to why it works. Nachtmahr no longer reads as one central figure surrounded by secondary decoration. There are several simultaneous points of attention across the stage, and the movement between them gives the performance much of its tension. The musicians maintain the structural discipline, while the women in the production are integral to the stage language rather than simply ornamental additions. Their choreography, posture and interaction reinforce Nachtmahr’s play with authority and submission. They contribute to the sense of order, but also to its deliberate instability. The more precisely the stage is arranged, the more excessive the activity in front of it can become. And the audience went completely wild. Not “wild” merely because people were dancing hard. What happened was cumulative. The room became denser at the front, hands were constantly raised, bodies moved forward, and the separation between active participants and passive spectators progressively disappeared. Every successful exchange with the stage seemed to authorise a larger response. That is why “madness” is both tempting and slightly inadequate as a description. The apparent madness had an architecture. It was being built. Rainer had explained in our interview that his band and crew remove much of the need for conscious control once he is onstage, allowing him to respond instinctively and become absorbed in the energy coming back from the room. He wanted the same for the audience: a framework reliable enough that people could safely lose themselves inside it. “I have a wonderful band and crew who take the need for control out of my hands, so I can completely let go onstage and simply become one with the energy of the crowd.” Wrocław demonstrated exactly what he meant. Bagger 258 and Cygnosic had already brought the audience a considerable distance. Nachtmahr did not have to spend the opening part of the set manufacturing involvement. They could begin by directing something already in motion. From there, the room became increasingly feral. One of the most striking aspects of a Nachtmahr show remains this gap between what the imagery appears to promise and what the live experience actually produces. Onstage there is hierarchy, command and discipline; in front of it, the effect is strangely collective. The imagery separates roles, while the music dissolves them. People move together. The stricter the construction onstage became, the less restrained the audience appeared. And in the middle of all that force came one of the evening’s most delicate moments. Thomas Rainer took time to remember Witek Kopytko, our colleague and a deeply valued member of the scene, who passed away earlier this year. He distributed tiny toy horses among people in the audience in Witek’s memory. It was a small, personal gesture, but precisely because nothing about it was inflated into spectacle, it carried real emotional weight. For those of us who knew Witek, worked alongside him or simply shared this scene with him over the years, the moment briefly changed the emotional temperature of the room. The concert had been built around movement, control and physical intensity; suddenly there was space for affection and remembrance. It was a genuinely beautiful tribute to a colleague who is very much missed. It also said something important about what these scenes actually consist of. Bands, promoters, journalists, photographers and audiences may occupy different roles at an event, but over years those roles begin to overlap into a community. Remembering one of its people in the middle of such a large production was not a detour from the evening. It belonged there. When the music resumed, the contrast only made the final part of the set more pronounced. The machinery returned, the crowd returned to movement, but the evening had briefly revealed something much softer underneath it. The setlist Rainer’s description of the setlist as dramaturgy becomes particularly interesting when looking at the stage sheet from Wrocław. New IMPERIVM material was not placed into an isolated promotional block; it sat among songs from different periods of Nachtmahr’s catalogue. With the clearly crossed-out alternatives on the photographed sheet omitted, the visible running order was: Wer Wind sät, Keine Lieder, Weil ich’s kann!, Liebst du mich?, Tanzdiktator, Stärker als ihr Hass, Sirenen, Heile mich, Die Straße, Kampfbereit, Beweg dich!, “Mädchen in Uniform“, Unterwerfung, Der Schlaf, Katharsis. Ending on “Katharsis” was especially fitting. By that stage, the idea had already been enacted physically for well over an hour. Wrocław, and what comes next There was something especially satisfying about watching all of this happen here. Wrocław has been remarkably well served by dark music this autumn, and the concentration of good bookings is beginning to change the rhythm of the city’s scene. It matters that international industrial, EBM, darkwave and gothic artists are not simply appearing as occasional exceptions but arriving regularly enough for audiences to develop continuity between events. That continuity is important because nights like this depend on difference as much as similarity. Bagger 258 took familiar EBM mechanics and made them feel immediate, aggressive and highly physical rather than nostalgic. Cygnosic widened that physicality into something more fluid, melodic and atmospheric. Nachtmahr then absorbed everything accumulated during the previous sets and used it as raw material for a performance based on reciprocal escalation. The Polish IMPERIVM opening continues with Poznań at Pod Minogą on 2 October and Warsaw at VooDoo Club on 3 October, before the tour moves on internationally. Their debut album “Aufwärts gehts bergab” was released in February 2026 and includes remixes by Nachtmahr, NordarR and Menticide; Side-Line covered the album in a March 2024 interview with the duo. Cygnosic is the Athens-based dark-electro project of Georgios Psaroudakis. “Demystify” appeared in 2023 as the project’s seventh full-length album, while 2025’s “Theorem” revisited Cygnosic compositions through metal arrangements without abandoning the project’s electronic core. Side-Line first covered the Nachtmahr connection in 2019, when Cygnosic toured with Nachtmahr and labelmates C-lekktor behind the “Epiphany” LP. Nachtmahr, founded by Austrian musician Thomas Rainer in 2007, has developed a distinctive language around hard electronic rhythm, theatrical authority, confrontation, discipline and increasingly broad stylistic freedom. IMPERIVM is the latest stage of that development, while the current tour is the largest and longest undertaken under the Nachtmahr name. The Wrocław opening showed how carefully the three-band construction worked: Bagger 258 established the body, Cygnosic changed the way it moved, and Nachtmahr took control of what had already been set in motion. By the end, the contradiction Thomas Rainer and I had discussed before the tour, extreme control on one side of the stage and deliberate surrender on the other, no longer needed explaining. It was visible everywhere in the room.

items.body: This album from the Danish project Black Vault was actually released quite some time ago—back in the spring of 2025. With the telling title “Death Obsessed”, we are presented with five tracks. There is no room for fun in this sonic universe; instead, we are confronted with a dark, nihilistic-sounding whole. The atmosphere is carefully constructed and accentuated by occasional spoken-word samples, creating a tormented listening experience. Blending elements of Dark-Ambient, Industrial, Noise, and even Ritual music, the production is sometimes a tiny chaotic yet undeniably well-crafted. The combination of influences is fascinating, and, to my mind, the opening two tracks are particularly compelling. Black Vault transports us into an illusory world of ruin. The only thing missing, for me, is an absolute climax—though that certainly doesn’t mean this isn’t a great record. (Rating:7½). Listen to “The Hollow Sighs Of Putrid Emission”: The Hollow Sighs Of Putrid Emission by Black Vault About Black Vault Black Vault is a Danish project working in occult industrial and death-industrial territory on the German label Dunkelheit Produktionen. The project’s debut album, “Hymns To The Great Devourer”, was released on Dunkelheit Produktionen in 2023. “Death Obsessed” is the follow-up, recorded between 2023 and 2024 and released on March 1, 2025, mixed and mastered by Grant Richardson at Hex Audio Labs.
items._cn_summary: 丹麦项目Black Vault的第二张专辑《Death Obsessed》由德国地下厂牌Dunkelheit Produktionen发行，收录五首作品，构建出一片黑暗虚无的声学宇宙。专辑融合暗氛围、工业、噪音乃至仪式音乐的多种元素，以偶尔出现的人声采样强化听觉折磨感，整体制作在混乱与精密之间取得平衡。前两首曲目被认为尤其出色，将听众带入一片幻灭的废墟世界。唯一的遗憾在于缺少一个绝对的高潮时刻，但并不妨碍其作为一张扎实作品的成立。录音跨越2023至2024年，由Grant Richardson在Hex Audio Labs完成混音与母带处理。

items.body: Dreams may be among the strangest territories available to us. Each night, the mind constructs worlds without asking permission from physics, geography, biography, or common sense. We meet people who never existed, return to places that vanished years ago, fall in love with strangers, lose ourselves, recover ourselves, and wake carrying the emotional residue of events that never occurred. There is something almost miraculous in this private universe, because within it we are briefly released from the limits imposed by circumstance. Thought offers a similar freedom. We can imagine nearly anything, even when reality permits us to accomplish only a fraction of it. For Venus Volcanism, the Iceland-based project of Crete-born vocalist, musician, and producer Rena Rasouli, dreams become both refuge and research subject. Her new song, “Dreams,” inhabits the uncertain region between waking life and the private worlds that continue behind our eyes. Rasouli created the song exactly one year ago as the first snow settled across the peaks surrounding Siglufjörður, Iceland’s northernmost town. She keeps a journal beside her bed, recording complete dreams when possible and preserving stray images when that is all sleep leaves behind. Before sleeping, she gives herself a small invocation: “As I close my eyelids and sleep takes me, gently or not, please show me something that will help me understand myself a little better.” Dreams drifts somewhere between dark pop, ambient composition, experimental electronics, and neoclassical music, with affinities to This Mortal Coil, Julee Cruise, Penelope Trappes, and Zola Jesus. Rasouli’s voice occupies the center while drones, synthesizers, arpeggiated figures, and suspended textures create an unstable sense of location. Beauty and unease coexist. The song seems to hover between desire imagined and desire remembered. Its love story belongs to an imaginary lover, though imagination hardly makes the emotion less consequential. Desperation, longing, idealization, and obsession can become perfectly real experiences even when their object remains beyond reach. “Have you ever found yourself dreaming with your eyes open? I honestly don’t know how many times I have done it while diving into Icelandic pools,” says Rasouli. “Especially during winter, I feel like I am balancing somewhere between the conscious and the unconscious, and sometimes I don’t even know how the day has passed. I am and I am not. I exist and I do not exist. I do everything I am supposed to do; I move through the day as I should, but if you know me well enough, you might see it in my eyes: I am somewhere in between.” This suspended condition also governs the video, directed by Tassos Gkoletsos with help from friends and members of the Siglufjörður community. Northern Iceland’s long winter darkness turns ordinary routines into strange repetitions: tending plants, bathing, working, exercising, moving through familiar rooms while another existence unfolds internally. “During those months, I always find myself somewhere in between,” Rasouli continues. “I do everything I need to do and I’m relatively functional, but everything feels like autopilot. At the same time, another scene is taking place inside my head. I dream and imagine other things while going through the ordinary routines of everyday life, like watering my plants, having my bath, working, and going to the gym.” Perhaps this is why Dreams feels so intimate. Rasouli treats imagination as a parallel dimension of daily existence, one without measurable coordinates yet capable of altering everything that happens after we return. items.body: The screams of children, far away Echo in this perfect day A perfect society becomes considerably harder to admire once somebody explains who has been paying for it. In Ursula K. Le Guin’s The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas, an entire city’s happiness depends upon the suffering of a single child, an arrangement its citizens learn to accept as the price of their good fortune. There is plenty of room for horror in that cheerful consensus, especially once the people benefiting from it begin explaining why things simply have to be this way. Bologna’s La Mano Sinistra, whose name means “the left hand” in Italian, take up that ugly bargain on their debut single, Unnecessary Perfection. The track introduces Omelas, a seven-track concept album due November 6, 2026, through Bat-Cave Productions, translating Le Guin’s ethical dilemma into gothic rock with enough melodic momentum to carry its uncomfortable questions straight onto the dancefloor. A heartbeat rhythm opens the track, its alternating accents pressing against sustained, cold synthesizer tones before a thick, low-slung bassline sends everything forward. Guitar and electronics give the melody a generous sweep while Davide Sacco sings with the decadent authority of a frontman who can make a warning sound almost inviting. The combination brings to mind The Danse Society around their Heaven Is Waiting era, with something of Children on Stun and Brotherhood of Pagans in the vocal delivery and the way the instruments lock together. The guitar break ascends and descends through the melody, supplying an exhilarating lift while sustaining the chill of the surrounding synths. When Sacco’s voice returns alongside it, a more romantic quality enters his timbre, adding a strange tenderness to the accusation. This is the kind of gothic rock that makes getting dressed to go out feel like the opening scene of an evening full of possibilities. For a song about the moral cost of everybody having a good time, it has a wicked talent for getting the evening started. The lyrics initially survey a population blessed with sharp minds, untouched lives, and the promise of a cure for all, while concealed currents move beneath that reassuring surface. Sacco’s recurring question, “What’s necessary, what is not,” unsettles the supposed inevitability of the arrangement. By the closing lines, children’s screams carry across the distance into the perfect day itself. Read alongside Le Guin’s story, that distance becomes part of the accusation: comfort depends upon keeping suffering far enough away to be tolerated, even when its beneficiaries know exactly what sustains their happiness. The band describe the single this way: “The paradox of perfection. A fast-paced, impactful track reflecting the fictitious tranquility of a society built upon the distant screams of the weakest.” The accompanying video gives that selective vision an effective visual counterpart. High-contrast black-and-white performance footage is crossed by horizontal bands that repeatedly interrupt faces, instruments, and the lyrics appearing on screen. Close-ups of hands working the strings alternate with Sacco at the microphone, while the bars make even the plainest words momentarily difficult to see. The treatment suggests an uncomfortable connection between an obstructed image and a society accustomed to accepting a partial view. Watch the video for Unnecessary Perfection below: La Mano Sinistra brings together Sacco on vocals and lyrics, Gianluca Lo Presti of Nevica on bass and electronics, and Giuseppe Lo Bue of Caron Dimonio on guitar and electronics. Sacco is also a co-founder of the contemporary theatre company ErosAntEros and artistic director of POLIS Teatro Festival, a background that gives the project’s theatrical character a clear foundation. Omelas grew out of Sacco’s stage production of The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas, performed by actress Eva Robin’s. Recorded at Loto Studio in Ravenna during the summer of 2025, the album develops its source material across seven chapters, addressing indifference, collective guilt, and the decision to abandon a prosperity built upon injustice for an uncertain life beyond it. Unnecessary Perfection is available on digital platforms. Omelas follows on November 6, 2026, via Bat-Cave Productions. items.body: Rosetta Stone Executing Nostalgia Cleopatra Records Despite Porl King’s formal reactivation of the Rosetta Stone name happening a full seven years ago, it’s been remarkably tricky to pin down a specific sound or approach which has defined this era of King’s work. There have been reappraisals of interregnum work under the miserylab handle, syntheses of classic Rosetta Stone songwriting and modern production, and a suite of covers delivered with characteristic dryness which blurs the line between irony and earnestness. New release Executing Nostalgia embraces this amorphous fluidity, jamming all of King’s angles on goth rock into a dense forty minute listen. Without meaning to play armchair psychologist, I’d credit much of this restlessness to the question of King squaring the large bodies of work he recorded under the miserylab and Death It Ends from 2007 to 2018 with the idea of a “return” to Rosetta Stone. The legacy of In Death It Ends in particular may have been the key all along; from the moment a mesh of misty distorted guitar miasma joins the weighty, doomily reverbed bass and resigned, muttering vocals of opener “Shadowban”, that project’s unmistakable mix of classic darkwave and witchhouse is conjured up. There it remains for the remainder of the A-side of original material, mixed into spindly early Sisters fog machine goth on “Someone”, blended with miserylab minimalism on “Regression”, and compounded upon itself on the Soft Moon-like echoes of “Negative”. On the flip side, a set of five covers also sounds well-integrated and cooked down. Earlier tributes (“The Witch”, “Sisters Are Doing It For Themselves”) hinged upon deft yet tongue slightly in cheek elevations of naff source material to Rosetta Stone’s original, ornately stormy sound, but in choosing a set of ur-goth and relatedly dark tracks for Executing Nostalgia‘s back half, that issue vanishes. These are clearly tunes which helped shape King’s youthful tastes, and whether it’s the tempestuous “Incubus Succubus”, the high camp of the Prunes’ “Pagan Love Song”, or the sly shadowcraft of Colin Newman’s oft-overlooked “Alone”, they’re delivered forthrightly. From a purely musical perspective at this point in the Rosetta Stone reboot, opting to close the record with the looping, machine-like rhythmic punch of The Lorries’ “Talk About The Weather” is a subtle masterstroke. Partially made up of the sort of sparse clatter and jangle associated with miserylab but shot through with the sort of impassioned vocal vitriol which illuminated early Rosetta Stone material and the right winding guitar to suit, King’s version is almost slavishly true to the original, yet in that manner it draws together just about all the corners of his various epochs, a fitting marker of Rebooting Nostalgia‘s everything and the kitchen sink approach. Buy it. Executing Nostalgia by Rosetta Stone The post Rosetta Stone, “Executing Nostalgia” appeared first on I Die: You Die.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Porl King重启Rosetta Stone后的新作，将他过去十余年间在miserylab和Death It Ends等项目中的不同美学路径整合进同一张唱片。A面原创作品混合了经典暗潮的阴郁氛围、witchhouse的迷雾质感以及minimalism式的简约骨架，在失真吉他、低沉贝斯与喃喃人声之间构建出统一的听觉基调。B面五首翻唱曲目选取了早期goth与相关黑暗场景的经典作品，涵盖了The Prunes的戏剧化、Colin Newman的狡黠暗影以及The Lorries的机械节奏循环，后者作为收尾巧妙地将作者各个时期的创作特征串联起来。整张专辑呈现出一种不安定的流动性，既是对个人音乐遗产的回顾，也是对goth rock传统在当代语境下如何延续的一次整合性尝试。

振付（家）と権力構造。振付を「ナンセンスなゲームのルールの恣意性」へと還元する自己批判。スペクタクルとして消費される身体からの逃走。バレエという制度が内包するダンサーのヒエラルキー、さらには訓練されたプロのダンサー／アマチュアや子ども、障害者といった出演者のヒエラルキーの解体。「ダンスとは何か」について脱構築するようなコンセプチュアルな作品を制作してきたフランスの振付家ジェローム・ベル。自身の名前をタイトルに冠した本作『ジェローム・ベル』は、約30年に渡る振付家としてのキャリアと人生を振り返り、映像を見せながら自作について解説し、創作の背後にあるダンスや社会への問いを語る、2時間のレクチャー・パフォーマンスである。また、2019年以降は、環境負荷への配慮から、ベルと彼のカンパニーは飛行機での移動を行なわず、上演地ごとに、現地のパフォーマーがその土地の言葉で演じる形を採っている。日本版では、2025年の YPAMでの上演と同様、川口隆夫が「ジェローム・ベル」として出演する。「他者による代演」というもうひとつの仕掛けについては後編で詳述し、まずは本作で語られるベルの思索の軌跡を概観してみよう。 10代後半で国立ダンス学校に進学するも、従順なダンサーの養成機関にすぎないことへの失望。「踊らない」ダンサーの演劇的な仕草で観客に感銘を与えることができるピナ・バウシュの舞台に力づけられたこと。当時の1980年代は、ミッテラン大統領の進歩的な左派政権下でダンスに対する国家的支援が拡充され、コンテンポラリー・ダンスが盛行した。海外ツアーにも多く参加し、ダンサーとして華やかな経歴だったが、親友2人をエイズで亡くし、「人生で何をやりたいのか」という問いに直面したことから、振付家になろうと決心する。 ここでベルが特異なのは、振付家になるための修行期間として、2年間、美術史、文学、哲学などの読書に専念したことだ。その際、「アート」「文学」という言葉を「ダンス」に置き換えて読む。例えば、ロラン・バルトの『零度のエクリチュール』を「零度のダンス」に置換し、「ダンス」を問い直す思考のフレームを鍛える。また、ギー・ドゥボールの『スペクタクルの社会』に触発され、消費者の目を惹きつけるためにメディアが誇張する（性的）魅力に溢れた身体表象を批評するため、ダンスの媒体（メディウム）である身体を即物的な次元で扱う。本作と同じタイトルで発表された初期作『ジェローム・ベル』（1995）では、全裸のダンサーが、初めて触るものであるかのように自分自身の皮膚をつまみ、限界を確かめるようにゆっくりと皮を伸ばすシーンが紹介される。また、衝撃的なのが、舞台のみならず、日常的な社会規範からも「身体を解放」するために、ダンサーが放尿するシーンだ。全裸のダンサーは不動のまま、身体の内部にあったものが外に放出され、重力によって落下する運動が提示される。 観客の拒絶や批評家の酷評にもめげず、ベルはさらにラディカルな創作を進めていく。代表作のひとつ『The Show Must Go On』（2001）では、スペクタクルの消費社会と振付という権力への自己批評を展開。世界的にヒットしたポップ・ソングの歌詞を「振付のスコア」と捉え、特定の歌詞が流れた時だけ、ダンサーは歌詞が指示する行為を行なう。例えば、デヴィッド・ボウイの「レッツ・ダンス」がかかると、「レッツ・ダンス」と歌われるサビの間だけ、出演者はクラブ風の踊りを繰り返すが、それ以外は棒立ちの異様な時間が続く。ポリスの「見つめていたい」が流れると、出演者は舞台前面に一列に並び、客席を黙って凝視する。高尚なダンス／ポップ・カルチャーというヒエラルキーや、「見る／見られる」の非対称性の解体と同時に、ムーブメントの審美性や高度なテクニックが排除され、「振付とは、身体に課されたゲームのルールにすぎない」という恣意性や権力性が露わになる。 また、ベルは2000年代以降、パリ・オペラ座バレエ団からの依頼（！）を契機に、ダンサー自身が実演を交えて自伝を語る「ドキュメンタリー・ポートレート」のシリーズに取り組む。アマゾンの先住民の部族をフィールドワークしたクロード・レヴィ＝ストロースの文化人類学を参照し、「バレエという未知の体系」が研究対象にされた。調査サンプルとして起用されたのが、バレリーナのヴェロニク・ドワノーだ。バレエ団のヒエラルキーでは中間に位置するドワノーは、主役のエトワールを引き立てるために舞台美術のように静止する時間が最も辛いと語り、群舞と静止を行き来するシーンを実演してみせる。『白鳥の湖』の優美な音楽が覆い隠していたのは、ダンサーを非人間的な部品に変えるバレエの階級制度と、その基盤にある国家権力（絶対王政期に設立された王立ダンスアカデミー）だ。 ［Documentation Team © 2026 Hot Summer in Kyoto］ 2010年に入ると、ベルは、知的障害者の団体から依頼され、「言葉で表現することが難しい出演者とともに、人間性を疎外せず、どう創作できるか」という困難な問いに向き合う。『The Show Must Go On』のメソッドを応用しつつ、「出演者が自分の好きな曲を選び、自身のソロを作って踊る」という委ね方を選択した。踊りに熱中する出演者たちのパワーに圧倒され、「今、ここ」を生きている身体ほど舞台においてパワフルなものはないと語るベルは、『Disabled Theater』というタイトルとは裏腹に、この作品では、振付家という特権性からの解放、社会規範を解除する場として立ち上がる舞台、そして社会で周縁化された存在に表現力という力と武器を与えるものであったと振り返る。 『Disabled Theater』は高く評価されたが、「一人ひとり違うはずなのに、知的障害者としてひとくくりにされてしまう」という反省から、車椅子ユーザー、子ども、クィア、移民、定年退職者などより多様な出演者とともに、同じ手法でつくり上げたのが『Gala』（2015）である。また、『Disabled Theater』では、中央でソロを踊る出演者を、他の出演者が椅子に座って見つめるという構造だったが、『Gala』では、ソロの踊り手の動きを真似して他の出演者も一緒に踊ることにより、ソロ／群舞という境界も流動化させた。「それぞれが個でありながらどう平等でいられるか」という複雑な方程式をダンスで解くことの喜びがあったとベルは語る。 そして、イサドラ・ダンカンの自伝を元に彼女についての伝記的な作品をつくったことを契機に、ベルは、自身について語るこの作品『ジェローム・ベル』をつくるに至ったと語る。ダンスをめぐるラディカルな思索が2時間に凝縮された本作はそれだけでも十分に面白いのだが、さらにもうひとつの仕掛けが加算される。ここまで「ベルは」という主語で述べてきたが、実際に本上演で「ジェローム・ベル」として登場するのは、本人ではなく、川口隆夫という日本人のパフォーマーが日本語で語る。直接的な契機は気候変動対策であるとベルは述べるが、「本人ではない他者が振付家の自伝を語る」という構造は、「振付」それ自体についてのさらなる問いを推し進める。それは同時に、ダンス（舞台芸術）の反復性・再現可能性や、映像アーカイブと舞台芸術の一回性の問題についても問う作業になるだろう。 鑑賞日：2026/08/05（水） 関連レビュー 越智雄磨『コンテンポラリー・ダンスの現在──ノン・ダンス以後の地平』｜高嶋慈：artscapeレビュー（2020年07月15日号） 未だ見ぬ身体へ──川口隆夫『大野一雄について』｜岡村恵子：フォーカス（2017年11月15日号） ジェローム・ベル『ザ・ショー・マスト・ゴー・オン』（The Show Must Go On）｜木村覚：artscapeレビュー（2011年12月01日号） （後編へ）※10/5公開予定

items._cn_summary: 法国编舞家杰罗姆·贝尔的同名讲座表演登陆京都，以两小时回顾其三十年创作生涯。作品将编舞还原为「对身体施加的任意游戏规则」，对芭蕾等级制度、舞者阶级以及专业与业余的分野进行持续解构。早期作品《杰罗姆·贝尔》以全裸舞者放尿等极端场景直面身体解放议题；《The Show Must Go On》将流行歌词作为动作指令，在棒立与舞蹈的交替中暴露舞蹈媒介的任意性。《Disabled Theater》与《Gala》进一步以委身创作方式让智障人士、退休者、移民等边缘群体自主编舞，挑战「编舞家特权」与「独舞与群舞」的传统分界。文本中融入了罗兰·巴特、居伊·德波、列维-斯特劳斯等理论资源，使表演成为思辨性极强的跨学科实践。本次日本版由川口隆夫以本地语言代为呈现，构成「他人代演」的另一重实验机制。

items.body: Wardruna’s wonderful performance at London’s Union Chapel was a heavy vision of their might and majesty. One unstoppable note became a potent portal, leading to other, northern realms brimming with the threat of fire and the glimmer of ice. Their performance was an almost transcendent experience rooted in Norse spiritualism and the elements of fire, water and earth. This wasn’t Norway (they played two nights here as part of their European tour), but it could’ve been. The music was somehow both ancient and contemporary, sculpted by sharp blades and fearsome weaponry. It was also equally founded in love: for music, for tradition, for culture, for people. It fed on its own history and drank from the cup of the present, standing partly in lost centuries and partly in new, fertile ground, and that came across with every ground-pounding thump of a deer-hide drum. At first, a pair of gigantic horns flanked the stage, looking like great monuments that should be worshipped and respected, each one presenting a gate to be entered. One note can open everything, and the vocals soon lit up the space like a set of stark torches; together they carried a flame that burnt brightly. Harmonies came into being, with both Einar Selvik’s and Lindy Fay Hella’s all-encompassing vocals soaring to stratospheric levels and then diving deep into the earth. Materialising out of the earth was a dark kind of Nordic folk, but enriched with elements that were beyond classification. The music was full of power and passion, somehow older than everything else and yet incredibly fresh. At one point, faces were lit in the crimson of blood, like the prom scene from Carrie. The stringed instruments plucked out melodies composed of the lightest air, while other melodies flicked tongues of fire that tasted like copper and spewed out jets of molten flame. The lyrics glowed like warm flares against the Nordic night. The heavy, marching drums were like the racing hooves of ten thousand horses, all honing in on a certain, key point. It was the sound of war, the sound of battle, with music being the weapon. The chilly and piercing sound of a goat horn punctured the air, and the red-blooded, thunderous drums wound themselves up again, ready to pump more energy into the steady pounding of a restless heart. Other genres use these rhythms a lot, too – rhythm is just as crucial in today’s modern-era of house and electronic music as it was a thousand years ago and even earlier – but sometimes other, additional rhythms were woven in, making them ornate, complex and deep. Rain and thunder became an ominous premonition in the sound, the horn slowly drowning under the weight of a rain-drenched harmony that was as black as the night. The lyrics were conductors of heat and protectors against the cold air. Robed shadows lit up the walls, and like a procession of spirits from the past they marched in place, absorbing into the swelling harmonies, the stark intervals and the intensely delivered lyrics. Nothing was held back, because music such as this can never be tamed. The only way to truly experience it is to fully unleash it, to have the hood that covers its skull pulled back, revealing its face. The music reached an unstoppable, mighty crescendo before a scream that could tear flesh from bone shattered the air, but even among the more intense segments there were always moments of contemplation and relative peace – a period of change and calm – brought forth by a slower tempo or more of a sobering atmosphere. Something was always brewing, though. Strobing lights dazzled the audience and circular orbs of a softer light stretched their arms up to the heavens. Smoky, shrill horns and a steady, slow drum helped to shape a dense and ever-shifting atmosphere. This was the ultimate offering and another testimony to the power of music – songs of life and songs of death, songs of every experience, uniting everyone with their potency. It was an emotional performance that at times bordered on the euphoric. The final song was one about death, but it was also about our place in this life. It wasn’t a solemn ending but a triumphant one, a reassurance that the spirit of the music will always live on and embrace come what may, even after the soul has departed. Wardruna have a warm love for London and the city responded in kind with a lengthy standing ovation which the music and the performing artistry fully deserved. Photos: Nick Sayers www.wardruna.com www.unionchapel.org.uk
items._genre: nordic folk / ritual ambient / world music
items._cn_summary: 这是Wardruna在伦敦Union Chapel演出现场的乐评。乐队将北欧异教精神与自然元素（火、水、土）融入音乐表演，鹿皮鼓、羊角号、弦乐与人声交织，构成古老而当代的声音景观。表演以巨型牛角装置作为视觉开场，人声如火炬点燃空间，低音鼓模拟万马奔腾的战场节奏，铜质金属质感与火焰意象反复出现。乐评特别提到节奏在千年间从仪式鼓点到现代电子音乐中的延续性，以及雨声、雷声作为预言性元素融入和声的做法。文字本身带有强烈的仪式感描述，将音乐体验比作穿越北境的入口，强调其超越分类的文化融合特质。

items.body: The broadly ambitious Generate Music is the Prism Quartet's latest project, featuring saxophonists Timothy McAllister (soprano), Zachary Shemon (alto), Matthew Levy (tenor), and Taimur Sullivan (baritone). Formed in 1984, their mission is �To place the saxophone in unexpected contexts, expand the repertoire through new commissions, and challenge audiences.� On this eleven-track, 86-minute set, they do just that. Tyshawn Sorey | Ursula Rucker | Diane Monroe This collection includes the quartet augmented by David Gilmore (Electric guitar), David Krakauer (Klezmer clarinet), Tyshawn Sorey (Drums and percussion), Reuben Rogers (Bass), Ursula Rucker (Vocals and poetry), Susan Watts (Trumpet and vocals), and Diane Monroe (Violin). Through modern jazz arrangements, improvisations,� and spoken word, they seek to �explore the historical, cultural, and creative ties between Black and Jewish Americans.� Generate Music by PRISM Quartet, D. Gilmore, D. Krakauer, D. Monroe, R. Rogers, U. Rucker, T. Sorey, S. Watts � The opening track references �A Griot and a Cantor,� the storyteller in West African culture and the worship leader in the Jewish faith. The sonic architecture arrives with �The Unknown Common Ancestor,� which jumps between a World Saxophone Quartet-inspired sound and klezmer music with clarinet and trumpet.� � Generate Music by PRISM Quartet, D. Gilmore, D. Krakauer, D. Monroe, R. Rogers, U. Rucker, T. Sorey, S. Watts The striking and authoritative voice of Ursula Rucker narrates �Requiem for AJ.� After a dramatic overture, it sets up the narrative tension that develops across the record. Rucker tells the story of the 1964 murders of civil rights activists James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner near Philadelphia, Mississippi. On the 60th anniversary of this American tragedy, Rucker explains that they went �to register black voters (sigh)� and then she asks us to: Look up the rest of the story if you care Do you... Care? Or do you just... Do you?� With tense dramatic irony, Rucker nonchalantly states, �Poets have queries,� and the recitation ends with emphatic repetition of �Do you?�� This ten-minute powerhouse also features the band at its best with Tyshawn Sorey�s swirling drumming and David Gilmore (not to be confused with his Pink Floyd namesake) offering one of his several fiery guitar solos. It makes a fitting single, representative of the in-your-face right-left punches of improvised jazz and honest stylized performance poetry. Generate Music by PRISM Quartet, D. Gilmore, D. Krakauer, D. Monroe, R. Rogers, U. Rucker, T. Sorey, S. Watts Highlighted throughout with bursts of klezmer, often seamlessly blended with funky jazz, the Jewish tradition is especially highlighted on �Lift Every Voice and Sing.� Originally debuted in 1900, this hymn by brothers John Rosamond Johnson and James Weldon Johnson has been called a �Negro national anthem.� Here it is translated into Yiddish by Joshua Woletzshky and sung by Susan Watts, featuring violin by Diane Monroe. �Shall I continue to lie about my sadness to keep you from yours?� asks Rucker on �Let�s All Gather & Go All Together, Shall We,� offering an optimistic way forward in a world of hate. She narrates the story of a young black man in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, who is murdered by a Jewish pharmacist, exposing grief but also a way to get beyond it. Here and throughout, the music comments, prods, replies, and exuberantly jams out. Powerful, virtuosic, and close to the bone, Generate Music keeps its promise and takes another giant step in the evolution of the Prism Quartet. "Let us gather and all go together" by Ursula Rucker Live at World Cafe, Philadelphia on June 8, 2024 Find the artist online. items._cn_summary: Prism Quartet 萨克斯四重奏联合多位客座音乐人，推出探索非裔与犹太裔美国人历史文化纽带的跨界专辑。十首曲目融合现代爵士即兴、克莱兹默传统、口语诗歌与现代作曲元素，David Krakauer 的克莱兹默单簧管与 David Gilmore 的电吉他形成鲜明对话，Tyshawn Sorey 的鼓击构建张力漩涡。Ursula Rucker 以戏剧性旁白串联叙事，讲述1964年民权运动悲剧。作品在学院派爵士框架内引入世界音乐与诗歌朗诵，呈现出严肃的文化议题与实验性音乐语言的结合，适合关注跨界即兴与社会议题表达的听众。

items.body:
After the OĽUN album I reviewed enthusiastically a while back, here’s the next project, again motivated and led by violinist/fiddler/composer Ján Kružliak Jr., continuing the rapprochement, indeed embrace, between Slovakia’s traditional music and its classical music. This time it reconnects the works of classical composers who were inspired by and drew on village musics with those traditional sources and styles.
Three ensembles are involved: the Spectrum Quartett led by Kru�liak with two violins, viola and cello; Nogaband, the traditional-style quartet of fiddles, contra (chording viola) and bass that’s led by fiddler and singer Michal Noga; and the female vocal group Ulijanky, plus guest singer Simona Hulejov�.
The majority of the tracks are interpretations of works by Slovak composer Eugen Suchon (1908-1993), with others from fellow-Slovaks Ilja Zeljenka (1932-2007) and Alexander Moyzes (1906-1984), and Hungarian B�la Bart�k (1881-1945) who did a lot of his very detailed collecting of folk music in Slovakia.
In each case the sources - musicians and locations in villages across Slovakia - are credited in the notes, and these arrangements and performances reconnect with the energy and traditional vocal sound of those sources.
In no way is this an orchestra-smoothed thing; this is gutsy, brilliantly played and sung music with all the spirit, skill and technique of traditional music, from players and singers who deeply understand and inhabit it. It’s a glorious piece of work, music to luxuriate in. There’s too much richness to begin to detail, but here’s a dip into a few moments to give the flavor. The tracks all have very long titles detailing their sources, so for brevity’s sake I’ll just give track numbers.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由小提琴家/作曲人Ján Kružliak Jr.主导，汇聚三组音乐人：弦乐四重奏Spectrum Quartett、民俗弦乐组合Nogaband以及女声演唱团体Ulijanky，核心议题是让斯洛伐克当代古典作品与产生它们的乡村民间音乐传统重新对接。曲目主要改编自斯洛伐克作曲家Eugen Suchoň、Ilja Zeljenka、Alexander Moyzes以及深入斯洛伐克采风的匈牙利作曲家巴托克的作品，每首曲目标注了采风来源地与乐人信息。编曲与演奏刻意避免管弦乐式的圆熟处理，保留了民间音乐原有的粗粝能量与人声质感。专辑呈现出古典文本与活态民间传统之间的并置与互证关系，对理解中东欧音乐源流具有参考价值。

items.body:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhythms, and accordion-based
bal-musette
flavors.
For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.

items.body:
According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items._cn_summary: 这是挪威Camilla Hole Trio的第二张专辑《Langs》，相比前作《Eventyrferd》中科幻合成器与传统素材的大胆嫁接，本作回归更为朴素的地面气质。核心乐器高音萨克斯天然带入爵士血脉，开篇曲《Springleik》取材自挪威西部传统舞蹈音乐。三位成员角色分配模糊，Egil Kalman的模块合成器与Knut Kvifte Nesheim的颤音琴作为色彩层叠加于贝斯与鼓的节奏支撑之上。音乐在固定旋律与即兴展开之间不断游走，Hole陈述主题后，Kalman以贝斯接替旋律线与萨克斯齐奏，Nesheim则将节奏进一步打开。即兴段落逐渐取代原有结构，末尾Hole再奏一次旋律收束全曲，体现了三重奏对传统挪威民间素材的开放解构态度。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items._cn_summary: 这是一张由瑞典小提琴手与两位挪威乐手组成的三重奏专辑，在挪威小厂牌Taragot发行。三位音乐人各自拥有跨越传统与现代的丰富履历：主奏者长期从事瑞典民间音乐研究与教学，另一位早在1970年代便参与挪威跨界先驱乐队，第三位则以鼓手与作曲家身份活跃于多类型项目。专辑选取斯堪的纳维亚传统舞曲旋律，却以室内乐式的亲密对话方式重新诠释，乐手之间不断交错、叠加、解构，音乐碎片化后又归于静止。评论将其比作易卜生戏剧中表层欢愉下隐藏的暗流，开篇选曲便暗示了水妖传说所代表的阴暗底色。这种对民间素材的去舞蹈化、深层探索方式，使作品超越了常规民谣范畴，进入实验性的领域。

items.body: Review by Hector Enrique — Shifting from the brutal to the delicate within a single song - one of the hallmarks that Opeth handled with ease - reached a turning point with the groundbreaking "Damnation" (2003), an album that almost entirely dispenses with the hostile sounds of extreme metal to embrace the most melodic aspects of '70s progressive rock. A risky decision that, despite initial concerns, demonstrated the band's versatility in moving confidently between different musical styles, while leaving fans and critics alike wondering about the direction the band would take in the future.With "Ghost Reveries" (2005), their eighth album, the Swedes once again use death metal as one of the fundamental elements of their sound, integrated with progressive components that are far more developed than in their previous works. Mikael �kerfeldt's demonic growls, the monolithic and dense guitar riffs of Peter Lindgren and �kerfeldt - which evoke extreme bands like Morbid Angel, the more experimental Tool, or the classic Black Sabbath, among others - and a powerful instrumental foundation alternate and blend with deep, clean vocals, crystalline acoustic elements, and Per Wiberg's hypnotic and cosmic keyboards, to construct a sonic tapestry of contrasts and shifts in intensity that moves naturally between ferocity and a hypnotic, enveloping melancholy."Ghost of Perdition", "The Baying of the Hounds" - featuring evocative Jon Lord-style organ - and the oriental-inspired "Beneath the Mire" unfold across expansive instrumental valleys and peaks that showcase the band's maturity, and find their full expression in "Reverie / Harlequin Forest" - featuring superb clean and harmonic phrasing by �kerfeldt - and, above all, in the ritualistic and intriguing "The Grand Conjuration" - reminiscent at times of Pink Floyd's "Echoes" - the album's finest moments.And the influence of "Damnation" is also present and can be felt in the tremulous "Atonement" and "Hours of Wealth," with their keyboards and a certain jazzy flair, and in the closing "Isolation Years," with its acoustic and dreamlike character, featuring �kerfeldt's whispering vocals and Lindgren's arpeggios, ultimately shaping the excellent "Ghost Reveries", one of Opeth's finest albums and standing alongside the iconic "Still Life" and "Blackwater Park".4/4.5 stars
items._genre: progressive metal / death metal / progressive rock
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑将死亡金属的极端咆哮与七十年代前卫摇滚的旋律质感并置，在暴烈与柔美之间频繁切换。吉他部分厚重密集，借鉴极端金属与经典摇滚的沉重感；键盘铺陈出催眠而宇宙感的氛围。器乐段落起伏广阔，融合东方色彩、管风琴质感的键盘以及爵士化的灵动段落。死亡金属嗓音与清澈人声、呢喃低语交替出现，编制上展现出明显的成熟度。评论将其与乐队最具标志性的几张作品并置，认为延续了前作所开启的探索方向，并在对立元素的有机融合上达到了新的高度。整体呈现出一张在猛烈与沉思之间持续游走的概念化作品。

items.body: Somewhere between the panic attack and the curtain call, Fiona’s Phobias have found a rather entertaining place to set up shop. Their six-track EP DEMOnS Vol. 1 dresses burnout, self-disgust, and impossible attachments in gothic metal, pop punk, and dark cabaret, with enough theatrical excess to suggest that the orchestra pit has opened directly into hell. The jokes have teeth, the guitars favor elaborate flourishes, and the people inside these songs keep discovering that their favorite distractions have become further reasons to worry. Formed in 2022, the project pairs the deliberately elusive Nikki L with vocalist Krisanna Marie, whose background includes Hatesex, Penis Flytrap, and burlesque fire Go-Go performance. Their own comparison of the working relationship to The Phantom of the Opera seems appropriate for music so fond of trapdoors and dramatic entrances. Marie’s ability to move from a knowing, almost conversational delivery into operatic gestures gives these elaborate arrangements a useful center: someone has to keep an eye on the audience while the scenery catches fire. Euphoria is Tragic starts with a chugging guitar figure planted between punk and metal, while Marie brings a retro rock directness to its catalogue of procrastination and depleted pleasure. Around the minute mark, the arrangement grows dense with baroque embellishment; a wiry solo takes on something of an electric violin’s bite. The bright momentum makes an effective companion to lyrics about getting bored with your own bad habits. “I feel my powers wane; a witch without her magic” supplies the perfect image for that particular exhaustion, when yesterday’s magnificent escape becomes today’s inability to answer an email. The theatrical scale expands on Play It Cool, which sets an almost lounge-like opening vocal against metal accents before breaking into a gallop. There is something of Malice Mizer’s baroque grandeur in the meeting of ornate arrangements and vocal melodrama, with the forward motion suggesting the carriage from Castlevania: Rondo of Blood racing toward Dracula’s front door. Beneath the spectacle lies a grimly familiar instruction: take your pill, eat your food, behave, and convince everyone that nothing is wrong. As Marie’s singing becomes more operatic, the pressure to appear composed turns increasingly sinister, eventually spilling into the song’s bloodied escape fantasy. Imaginary Sins brings piano, nimble bass, and busy drums into a crooked little cabaret before the heavier ornamentation takes over. Guitar flourishes answer the rhythm’s clipped figures, and goblin-like responses jostle Marie’s lead, as though every unwanted thought has secured a speaking part. Its funniest lyric finds the bodily absurdity inside a familiar wish: “Wishin’ I was pretty on the inside – But there’s just guts.” Jealousy, appetite, and self-absorption populate this ballroom of dancing demons, while the music’s constant activity makes obsession feel exhausting even at its most playful. The cover of Bang Bang, offered as an ode to Kill Bill, fits neatly among these accounts of love going horribly wrong. A Phantom-style organ opening and old-school metal guitar melody send the song toward the grand, charging territory of Bonnie Tyler’s Holding Out for a Hero. Its childhood games and adult abandonment acquire the dimensions of a stage tragedy, complete with an ornate guitar solo. Placed between the EP’s psychological grotesques, the familiar tune becomes another example of affection leaving somebody flat on the floor. Whispers and giallo-like synth tones introduce She Loves To Kiss That Doll, before sweeping guitars open the room around Marie’s voice. An operatic interlude, edged with chimes, suspends the heavier movement as she sings of attachment to a figure whose beauty depends on a terrible act of denial. Stuffing, cold hands, and the replacement of blood with a handsome face turn romantic idealization into physical horror. The return of the metal arrangement gives that revelation force, while the lyric’s eventual admission that he has long been dead makes the tenderness more disturbing than any decorative cobweb could manage. Closing track Bittersweet Darling begins with chilly piano and the worn texture of an old recording, then carries that melodic idea into a broad sweep of gothic guitar. Progressive tempo changes unsettle a romance conducted through black-and-white television images, broken mirrors, and the comfort of a boxed-up illusion. Its lover remains available because the screen can keep performing; the person watching has surrendered something harder to recover. By the final turn toward the knife and the closing credits, the song has brought the EP’s appetite for spectacle into uncomfortable proximity with self-destruction. Across DEMOnS Vol. 1, the sheer amount of decoration can crowd the stage, but Marie’s shifts in delivery and the songs’ sharply drawn situations keep the excess purposeful. Fiona’s Phobias are especially effective when a grotesque image exposes an ordinary humiliation: craving attention while avoiding people, mistaking possession for love, or spending all your energy on the thing that leaves you empty. They have given those contradictions a lavish production, and the casting department appears to have found plenty of monsters willing to sing. DEMOnS Vol. 1 is out now, released October 2 via Misophoniac Rabbit. Listen below and find the EP on Bandcamp and Spotify. items.body: Test Dept and the Welsh performance company Brith Gof release “Gododdin: 2026 Remaster” on 4 December 2026 via Artoffact Records. The set expands their 1989 album into a 3CD/1DVD box, alongside a separate red vinyl LP and a digital edition. “Gododdin” is based on Y Gododdin, the earliest surviving Welsh-language poem, written around 600 AD. It tells of 300 Celtic warriors who attacked 100,000 invading Angles and lost. Test Dept and Brith Gof first staged the piece as a live performance at an abandoned Rover car factory in Cardiff in December 1988, using 600 tons of sand, 50 trees and 30 wrecked cars on a set that flooded as the show went on. Further performances followed in 1989 in Italy, the Netherlands, West Germany and Scotland. The original 1989 studio album was produced by Ken Thomas at Jacobs Studios from Test Dept’s existing studio and field recordings, augmented with brass and wind courtesy of Brith Gof’s John E R Hardy and bagpipes from Alistair Adams. Paul Jamrozy’s voice runs alongside the Welsh-language vocals of Lis Hughes Jones. “Gododdin: 2026 Remaster” widens that original 7-track album with 19 tracks that have not previously been released. The first disc is a reworked version built from newly unearthed multitrack tapes of the early studio sessions, put together by Test Dept founder members Graham Cunnington and Paul Jamrozy during the summer of 2026. The second disc carries a live recording from one of the 1989 performances, staged in a quarry in Polverigi, Italy. The DVD holds a documentary from the period, with live footage and interviews with performers, academics and other experts. Compiled by Test Dept with input from Brith Gof members Lis Hughes Jones, John E R Hardy and Heike Roms, the set was remastered by Paul Lavigne at Kontrast Mastering. It comes in a 5-panel ecopak with a 24-page booklet of archival imagery and writing, including an essay by author and Test Dept researcher Alexei Monroe. The artwork for both the box and the separate red vinyl LP was redesigned by Paul Jamrozy and Stefan Alt (ant-zen); the vinyl edition carries the original album plus one previously unreleased track and a printed insert. Ahead of the box set, Test Dept released the advance single “Gwr a Aeth Gatraeth / Prologue (Early Studio Sessions, Reworked 2026)” on 2 October 2026, available on Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube. “Gododdin: 2026 Remaster” is the second in Test Dept’s ongoing series of archival reissues on Artoffact Records, who signed the band in 2025 for catalogue reissues and a new album. It follows the 4xCD “Industrial Overture: Studio & Live Recordings 1982-1985”, released a year earlier. Artoffact will also release new Test Dept material in 2027. A separate event ties into the reissue: Test Dept and Brith Gof take part in a discussion and Q&A about “Gododdin” at Chapter in Cardiff on 24 October, as part of the Experimentica festival’s 25th-anniversary programme. About Test Dept Test Dept formed in London in the early 1980s as an industrial music group built around live percussion on scrap metal and found objects. In 1988 and 1989, the band collaborated with the Welsh avant-garde theatre company Brith Gof on “Gododdin”, staging it first at an abandoned car factory in Cardiff and then on tour in Italy, the Netherlands, West Germany and Scotland. The 1989 studio album version was produced by Ken Thomas at Jacobs Studios. Test Dept returned to active release and performance in the 2020s. In 2025, the band signed to Artoffact Records for a series of catalogue reissues alongside a new studio album. The first of those reissues, the 4xCD “Industrial Overture: Studio & Live Recordings 1982-1985”, arrived in October 2025. “Gododdin: 2026 Remaster”, out 4 December 2026, is the second. Current members Graham Cunnington and Paul Jamrozy built new versions of the early “Gododdin” studio sessions for the reissue during the summer of 2026, working from recently unearthed multitrack tapes. Test Dept continue to tour, with confirmed UK and European dates running from October 2026 into the summer of 2027, and have a new studio album due via Artoffact in 2027. About Brith Gof Brith Gof is a Welsh performance company known for large-scale, site-specific theatre work that drew on Welsh history and language. Co-founded by figures including Mike Pearson, Lis Hughes Jones and Clifford McLucas, the company staged “Gododdin” with Test Dept in Cardiff in 1988, adapting the early Welsh poem Y Gododdin into a promenade performance inside a disused car factory. Hughes Jones, John E R Hardy and Heike Roms were directly involved in compiling “Gododdin: 2026 Remaster” alongside Test Dept.

items.body: What’s old is always new again. We got a full-blown nü metal revival on our hands, noise rock is arguably as popular as it’s ever been, and Myspace-era metalcore is getting about as many new releases from bands with members who were born around the same time the legends were laying the foundation. I was also recently reminded that fucking Greta Van Fleet exists for some godforsaken reason. For some other reason, I feel like we’ve just kinda skipped over a lot of good stuff. Where’s the grunge revival? Where’s the college-rock revival? Where’s the early post-punk revival? Where’s all the shit that sounds like it was made by people who hadn’t yet figured out what genre they were supposed to be in? Why does everyone nowadays sound so ready to be categorized?Well, Whippets make a case to step into these shoes, sounding something like Unwound by way of Dinosaur Jr. and Jay Reatard, or like Fugazi covering Dismemberment Plan and Siouxsie and the Banshees at the same time. They convey this volatile energy with writhing guitar leads that are often as eerie as they are anthemic, and tuneful bass in a rhythm section that paves the way for both their most unruly and airy moments. Much like their 2024 self-titled release, Whippets again flex their knack for melodies that get their hooks in your eardrums like velcro. No Skulls is every bit as fearless and without boundaries, gaining traction across a multitude of late 80s and early 90s soundscapes, regularly finding familiar touchpoints with the intuition to pull the rug at just the right time, or mix ‘n’ match influences in a way that’s as much “Aha!” as it is “What the fuck?” It’s like post-punk found the perfectly imperfect dancing partner in shoegaze, distraught while still finding an endearing footing, abrasive, oddly charming, and eyebrow-raising all at once.The video for album opener “These Woods” taps into a similar throwback, like it could’ve been dug out of a shoebox full of forgotten tapes and old zines. With a hazy camcorder look, sunbleached and spliced together with live footage, BMXers, scrapbook imagery, and other ’90s feels, it has the scrappy and surreal feel of something you might’ve stumbled across on MTV’s 120 Minutes at 1 a.m. It’s an appropriate visual companion, familiar enough to trigger a deeply buried memory, but weird enough to feel like you’ve never quite seen it before—and maybe even inspire a bad haircut.Check it out: No Skulls drops today, October 2, on wax and digital via No Coast Records.
items._genre: post-punk / shoegaze / noise rock / indie rock
items._cn_summary: Whippets乐队专辑《No Skulls》延续了2024年同名作品的脉络，将后朋克与自赏派、噪音摇滚熔于一炉。吉他主导线蜿蜒而不安，旋律既阴暗又朗朗上口，贝斯在节奏组中铺设出粗粝与轻盈的两极空间。乐评指出乐队横跨80年代末至90年代初的多重声音景观，借鉴Unwound、Dinosaur Jr.、Jay Reatard、Fugazi、Dismemberment Plan与Siouxsie and the Banshees等乐队的影响，却以直觉化的方式将它们重新拼接，既熟悉又出其不意。主打单曲《These Woods》的MV采用90年代风格的模糊录像带美学，BMX骑行与剪贴簿影像交织，营造出怀旧而超现实的视觉氛围。整张专辑体现出对类型边界的有意模糊，介于旋律性与噪音之间，态度鲜明且不拘一格。

items.tags: クラシック 現代音楽 intoxicate 2026 August クラシック 現代音楽 # リイシュー クラシック 里見暁美 松平頼暁
items.excerpt: 『ピアノ・ホライズン』に80年代の日本の音楽シーンを垣間見る。ローズからモールス信号のような単音の連打が聴こえ、クラヴィのクラスターが連打を断ち切る。ファンキーな音色にマイルス・デイヴィスの音楽のようだと感じるが、リズムにグルーヴが感じられるわけではない。松平頼暁がこのアルバムを企画したピアニスト里見暁美に書き下ろした“エリクサトーン”だ。しばらくしてピアノが緩やかに辿る下降音形が聴こえ、そこに時折りピアノからの異音が混じり、雨後のアスファルトから昇る蒸気のような音場が立ち上がる。藤枝守の“フォーリング・スケール第6番”だ。この二人の作品は〈表現内容よりも構造が強調〉されていると近藤譲はノートに記す。

items._cn_summary: 这张1981年的专辑聚焦日本当代作曲与实验钢琴的交汇地带。松平赖晓为里见晓美量身定制的'埃利克萨顿'以单音连击开场，节奏线条充满机能感却缺乏真正律动，近似放克音色与迈尔斯·戴维斯式气质的混搭，呈现出结构先于表达的创作思路。藤枝守的'下降音阶第六号'则走向另一端，钢琴缓慢勾勒下行旋律，间杂泛音与噪音，织体如雨后路面升腾的水汽般弥漫。近藤让在乐谱笔记中指出，两位作曲家的共同特征在于'结构被置于表达内容之上'，这使其作品与常规演奏会曲目拉开距离，更接近欧洲战后序列音乐与极简主义之间的美学地带。整体上是一张强调理性构建、听觉实验先于情感宣泄的专辑。

items.body: Sudan Dudan is a Norwegian duo, Marit Karlberg and Anders Erik R�ine, who have released four albums over the last twenty years. On M�rke refrenger , their fifth, they are joined by Hans Hulb�kmo and Magnus Skavhaug Nergaard, contributing instrumentally and with the production. There are eight songs on the album with accompaniment principally led by acoustic guitar, augmented by fiddles, langeleik, lyre, jaws harp and more. The opening track, �Gard og grind� (�Fence and gate�) is a fine introduction to what is to come: finger-picked acoustic guitar, fiddle, bass and snare-drum played with brushes leading into the harmonized vocal, together creating an alluring sound drawing the listener in. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The mood of the album, reflected in its title which translates as �Dark Refrains,� is not always dark, but most of the material, including the title track, certainly has a reflective quality. According to the press release �the lyrics smoulder with unease about the present and the future, while looking back to the myths and riddles of the past. They speak of the earth, the sun, the moon, stars and planets, of lost brothers, quarrelling sisters, loss and grief, of the power of imagination, and of the answers to the simplest and most difficult riddles.� The lyrics of all the songs, in Norwegian, are included in the sleeve notes and while a hasty online translation can aid with some understanding, the full meanings tend to remain cryptic, but there is a sense that words and music complement each other. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan For all its dark moodiness, M�rke refrenger does have its lighter moments. �Bagatelle� recalls and reinvents the melody of a well-known French song, adding some off-kilter harmonies, while �Rulleball� is more characteristically Norwegian, employing a vocal style known as tralling in which words are replaced by a vocalization of the melody, originally used to accompany dances when no instrument was available. No translation necessary there. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The final track �Skriften p� veggen� (�the writing on the wall�) features, for the only time on the album, electric guitar. The sound is deep and twangy, shades of Duane Eddy or a David Lynch soundtrack and it works very well. All in all a fine, imaginatively conceived and beautifully produced record, available as a download or vinyl. Find the artists online. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑来自挪威二人组Sudan Dudan，专辑名意为"黑暗副歌"。八首歌曲以原声吉他为核心，辅以小提琴、挪威传统乐器langeleik（古琴）、里拉琴、口簧等器乐伴奏，营造出沉思而富有北欧氛围的声响。开篇曲以指弹吉他、小提琴与刷子鼓引领和声人声，引人入胜。专辑整体偏暗调，但并非完全阴沉，部分曲目展现了轻盈的一面，如借用法国旋律重新演绎的《Bagatelle》，以及运用挪威传统tralling唱法的《Rulleball》。终曲首次加入电吉他，深沉而twangy的音色带有David Lynch配乐的气质。歌词以挪威语书写，围绕大地、星辰、神话与谜语展开，文字与音乐互为映衬。整体制作精良，想象力充沛，是一张独到而内省的北欧民谣之作。
